citation: Page 69 (Book Page): High velocity bullet... produces a temporary cavitation in soft tissues... Energy in the bullet is very high and it tends to dissipate in the surrounding tissues more effectively in radial fashion creating instant cavitation.

category: Explain mechanism of injuries to soft and bony tissues of head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: Describe the role of bone fragments as 'secondary projectiles' in firearm injuries.
back: When hit by high-velocity bullets, bone shatters; fragments displace explosively in multiple directions, creating secondary tracks away from the primary bullet path.
citation: Page 70 (Book Page): Bone fragments behave as secondary projectiles and spread in various directions causing many secondary tracks.

category: Explain mechanism of injuries to soft and bony tissues of head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: Why is the electrical pathway from head to foot considered the most lethal?
back: It traverses the brain stem, directly injuring vital cardiac and respiratory centers in the medulla.
citation: Page 65 (Book Page): From head to either foot... involves brain stem having vital cardiac and respiratory centers is the most dangerous.

category: Explain mechanism of injuries to soft and bony tissues of head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: List the four anatomical factors influencing the severity and appearance of a bruise.
back:
1. Force of blow.
2. Vascularity of part.
3. Tissue laxity (e.g., eyelids/lips).
4. Skin color.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): Factors influencing severity: 1. Force of blow 2. Vascularity of the part 4. Type of tissue (blood spreads easily in lax area around eye and lips) 6. Skin color.

category: Explain mechanism of injuries to soft and bony tissues of head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: How does tissue architecture differentiate blunt force outcomes on the head versus the buttocks?
back:
Head: Scalp stretched over bone produces lacerations due to compression. 
Buttocks: Abundant soft tissue (skin, fat, muscle) absorbs force effectively, usually producing bruises rather than skin breach.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Head has scalp stretched over a bone whereas buttock comprises mostly of soft tissues of skin, fat and muscles... on the head it shall produce a laceration, whereas similar impact on the buttocks shall produce a bruise.]

category: Explain mechanism of injuries to soft and bony tissues of head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: Describe the sequence of inner and outer table fractures in Rowhbotham's local skull deformation.
back:
1. Force forms a shallow cone.
2. Inner table at the apex stretches and fractures first.
3. Outer table at the periphery fractures subsequently.
4. Results in a comminuted depressed fracture.
citation: Page 61 (Book Page): [inner-table at the apex of the cone fractures before the outer table, whereas at the periphery the outer table fractures first... extension of the break... precipitating comminuted depressed fracture.]

category: Explain mechanism of injuries to soft and bony tissues of head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: Differentiate the primary anatomical locations for split lacerations versus over-stretch lacerations.
back:
Split: Sites where skin is firmly supported by underlying bone (scalp, forehead, chin).
Over-stretch: Areas where skin is loose and poorly supported (inguinal region, axilla).
citation: Page 58 (Book Page): [Split laceration occurs on scalp, forehead, chin or any other part of the body where skin is firmly supported by underlying bone... Over-stretch laceration is... where skin is loosely supported as in inguinal region.]

category: Explain mechanism of injuries to soft and bony tissues of head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: What soft tissue findings characterize a 'grinding compression' injury from an automobile wheel?
back: Multiple skin tears, separation of skin and muscle layers from bone, and extensive crushed tissue extravasation. High risk of fat embolism and renal failure.
citation: Page 58 (Book Page): [characteristics... are multiple skin tears; muscles are also separated from the skin and other underlying tissue... extravasations of blood... precipitate fat embolism.]

category: Explain mechanism of injuries to soft and bony tissues of head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: What is the physiological mechanism of immediate death during manual neck compression (throttling)?
back: Reflex cardiac asystole (arrest) triggered by stimulation of the carotid sinus or vagus nerve due to sudden variations in tension.
citation: Page 150 (Book Page): [Pressure on carotid sinus/vagus nerve, which gets stimulated and precipitates reflex cardiac arrest... increased tension... produces inhibitory circulatory effects.]

category: Explain mechanism of injuries to soft and bony tissues of head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: Which specific laryngeal structures are most vulnerable to fracture during indirect neck compression?
back: The greater cornue of the hyoid bone and the superior horn of the thyroid cartilage, particularly when calcified in older victims.
citation: Page 150 (Book Page): [Common sites of fractures are greater cornue of hyoid bone and superior horn of thyroid cartilage especially when calcified as in advanced age.]

category: Explain mechanism of injuries to soft and bony tissues of head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: How does abdominal organ consistency (solid vs. hollow) affect injury patterns in blunt trauma?
back:
Solid (liver/spleen): Rupture or shatter easily.
Hollow (stomach/bladder): Displace contents explosively as secondary projectiles if full of fluid; spongy organs (lungs) compress/absorb air shock.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Liver, spleen and kidney are solid... Lungs are spongy... Stomach, intestine... are hollow sacs having fluid... contents get separated into particles, which get displaced explosively.]

category: Explain mechanism of injuries to soft and bony tissues of head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: Contrast the mechanisms of long bone fractures produced by direct impact versus leverage.
back:
Direct: Bone fractures at the exact site of impact.
Leverage (Indirect): Force is diverted to a remote weaker point, often causing spiral or transverse fractures from twisting/pulling.
citation: Page 60 (Book Page): [Long bone fracture... occurs either at point of impact or bone acting as a lever divert the force to other remote weaker point... spiral fracture by twisting and transverse fracture.]

category: Explain mechanism of injuries to soft and bony tissues of head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: Describe the physiological hallmark of traumatic asphyxia resulting from chest immobilization.
back: Mechanical prevention of chest expansion causes anoxic anoxia, manifesting as acute facial/conjunctival congestion and a clear demarcation line above the pressure site.
citation: Page 155 (Book Page): [immobilization of chest... acute congestion of the face, conjunctivae and skin of the chest showing a clear demarcation between areas above the level of pressure.]

category: Explain mechanism of injuries to soft and bony tissues of head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: What is the defining mechanical effect of a high-velocity bullet striking soft tissue?
back: Temporary cavitation; kinetic energy dissipates radially, creating a vacuum/cavity significantly larger than the bullet diameter before the tissue recoils.
citation: Page 69 (Book Page): [High velocity bullet... produces a temporary cavitation in soft tissues... larger than the diameter of low velocity bullet... tissues recoil and collapse back leaving a permanent cavity.]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: What is the defining clinical feature of cerebral concussion following a head strike?
back:
• Transient period of loss of consciousness
• No apparent anatomical lesion on gross inspection
• May include minimal petechial hemorrhages in brain substance
citation: Page 89 (Book Page): [Cerebral concussion... is transient period of loss of consciousness... There are no positive findings in EEG and autopsy except a few petechial hemorrhages]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: Explain the mechanism of a depressed 'pond' fracture resulting from local skull deformation.
back:
• Localized force crushes outer table into diploe
• Inner table stretches and fractures at the cone apex
• Occurs when force exceeds bone strength
citation: Page 61 (Book Page): [Sequence of events at the site of impact is formation of a shallow cone. Apex of cone stretches the inner-table... both fracture... precipitating comminuted depressed fracture.]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: Contrast the clinical manifestation timing between acute and latent subdural hemorrhages.
back:
• Acute: Symptoms manifest within 24–48 hours (lethargy to coma)
• Latent: Slow leakage from perforating veins; can remain asymptomatic for months
citation: Page 91 (Book Page): [In acute, symptoms of compression manifest in about 24-48 hours... Latent form of subdural hemorrhage develops due to slow leakage... remains so for months or even years.]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: Why does sudden pressure on the carotid sinus during throttling cause immediate death?
back:
• Triggers reflex parasympathetic stimulation
• Stimulates the vagus nerve
• Results in immediate cardiac asystole (reflex cardiac arrest)
citation: Page 154 (Book Page): [Increase tension... Precipitates strong parasympathetic stimulation and produces inhibitory circulatory effects... sudden sympatho-adrenal or parasympathetic stimulation leads to circulatory failure, which proves fatal.]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: Which specific procedure is used during autopsy to demonstrate a traumatic pneumothorax?
back:
• Create a skin pocket at chest side
• Fill pocket with water and stab intercostal space
• Observe air bubbles replacing water in an inverted graduated cylinder
citation: Page 120 (Book Page): [An inverted graduated glass cylinder is held in the pocket containing water... stabbed with a scalpel below the water level... show gas bubbles replacing the water]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: List the anatomical findings that constitute a 100% loss of earning capacity in industrial injuries.
back:
• Loss of both hands or absolute deafness
• Double amputation through leg or thigh
• Total loss of essential eyesight
citation: Page 33 (Book Page): [Percentage loss of earning capacity... Loss of one hand and one foot... 100... Absolute deafness... 100]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: Describe the diagnostic significance of 'rice water stools' in acute abdominal arsenic poisoning.
back:
• Result of massive plasma transudation into intestinal lumen
• Coupled with mucosal irritation and hyperperistalsis
• Mimics clinical symptoms of cholera
citation: Page 172 (Book Page): [Bulk of transudes into the lumen of small intestine together with mucosal irritation... stimulates peristalsis leading to characteristic rice water stools.]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: Differentiate between hyoid bone fractures caused by throttling versus direct trauma.
back:
• Throttling: Indirect pressure through thyro-hyoid ligament (greater cornua)
• Direct Trauma: Direct blow (karate strike) usually fractures the hyoid body
citation: Page 150 (Book Page): [fractures by two mechanisms; direct pressure on bone and indirect pressure through thyro-hyoid ligament... fracture of body of hyoid bone... follows a direct blow like in karate.]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: Describe the pathophysiological progression of Crush Syndrome involving the limbs.
back:
• Severe muscle crushing releases myoglobin
• Myoglobin and granular casts obstruct renal tubules
• Results in renal ischemia and failure
citation: Page 84 (Book Page): [Crush syndrome... severe battering by police... Myoglobin and granular casts are seen in the tubules of kidney... eventual renal failure.]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: Why are 'greenstick' fractures specifically characteristic of limb injuries in children?
back:
• Higher bone elasticity in pediatric patients
• Force causes indentation and incomplete break on one side
• Often associated with Battered Baby Syndrome
citation: Page 60 (Book Page): [Long bones of children are comparatively more elastic and show less damage to only one side of bone... resulting in greenstick fracture.]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: Contrast the effects of a blunt strike to a stationary head versus a head in motion.
back: A strike to a stationary head usually produces localized scalp injury and fractures at the contact point. A head in motion involves 'contre-coup' mechanisms, often causing brain lesions distant from the impact site.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [A strike to a’stationary head will produce a local injury of the scalp at the site of contact... in the case of a head in motion hitting a stationary object, the resultant trauma to the head is called contre-coup... Lesion may not be symmetrical and intracranial hemorrhages to head.]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: What is the typical source and clinical course of an extradural hemorrhage?
back: Source: Rupture of the middle meningeal artery or vein, usually following a temporal fossa fracture. Course: Rapid accumulation of blood leading to a lucid interval followed by rapid compression and coma.
citation: Page 90 (Book Page): [The most common site of extradural hemorrhage is temporal fossa due to the rupture of middle meningeal vessels... Extradural hemorrhage in adults is exclusively traumatic.]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: Describe the mechanism and diagnostic markers of death by 'vagal inhibition' in neck injuries.
back: Mechanism: Reflex cardiac asystole caused by stimulation of the carotid sinus or vagus nerve. Markers: Immediate death with a total absence of typical asphyxial signs (like cyanosis or petechiae).
citation: Page 154 (Book Page): [Sudden sympatho-adrenal or parasympathetic stimulation leads to circulatory failure, which proves fatal... reflex cardiac asystole takes place due to variations of tension within carotid sinuses.]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: Identify the specific internal fractures associated with manual strangulation (throttling).
back: Classic fractures involve the greater cornua of the hyoid bone and the superior horn of the thyroid cartilage, especially in cases with calcified structures.
citation: Page 150 (Book Page): [Common sites of fractures are greater cornue of hyoid bone and superior horn of thyroid cartilage especially when calcified as in advanced age.]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: What defines 'Traumatic Asphyxia' and its characteristic facial appearance?
back: Definition: Immobilization of the chest (e.g., stampede) prevents respiration. Appearance: Intense facial cyanosis/congestion with petechiae, sharply demarcated above the level of chest pressure.
citation: Page 155 (Book Page): [Traumatic asphyxia is immobilization of chest and is always accidental... acute congestion of the face, conjunctivae and skin of the chest showing a clear demarcation betweenn areas above the level of pressure and one below.]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: Contrast the effects of blunt trauma on solid versus hollow abdominal organs.
back: Solid organs (liver, spleen, kidney) are prone to direct rupture or laceration. Hollow organs (stomach, bladder) suffer explosive rupture if impact occurs while they are distended with fluid.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Liver, spleen and kidney are solid... Stomach, intestine, heart, gall and urinary bladder are hollow sacs having fluid... which get displaced explosively in all directions away from the bullet path.]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: A victim presents with 'Grinding Compression' limb injuries. What specific systemic complication is expected?
back: Fat Embolism: Crushed adipose tissue releases fat droplets into the circulation, potentially occluding pulmonary or cerebral vessels, leading to rapid death.
citation: Page 58 (Book Page): [When grinding compression laceration occurs over wide area, they precipitate fat embolism... Fat droplets in pulmonary vessels.]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: Define 'Crush Syndrome' in the context of severe lower limb battering.
back: It involves renal failure caused by renal ischemia and the release of myoglobin/acid metabolites from crushed muscle, manifesting as swelling and tubular casts.
citation: Page 84 (Book Page): [Crush syndrome is a difficult medico legal problem, met in cases of industrial accidents or severe battering by police especially involving buttocks and lower limbs... Pigments like myoglobin and granular casts are seen in the tubules of kidney.]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: Under Pakistani Law, differentiate 'Itlaf-i-udw' from 'Itlaf-i-salahiyyat-i-udw'.
back: Itlaf-i-udw involves dismembering, amputating, or severing a limb/organ. Itlaf-i-salahiyyat-i-udw involves destroying the function/capacity of an organ or causing permanent disfigurement.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): [Itlaf-i-udw: Causing of dismemberment, amputation, severement of any limb or organ... Itlaf-i-Salahiyyat-i-Udw: Destroying of permanently impairing the function or capacity of an organ... or causing permanent disfigurement.]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: What are the three distinct categories of 'Post-Traumatic Amnesia' following head injury?
back: 1. Anterograde: Loss of memory extending forward from time of injury. 2. Retrograde: Loss of memory extending backward from time of injury. 3. Psychogenic: Forgetting due to psychological stress.
citation: Page 89 (Book Page): [Post-traumatic amnesia... is of two types: Antrograde amnesia extending forwards from the time of injury... Retrograde amnesia extending backwards from the time of regaining of consciousness.]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: What defines a post-traumatic concussion in head injuries?
back: A transient clinical state characterized by immediate loss of consciousness and reflexes following a strike to the head, occurring without anatomical lesions.
citation: Page 89 (Book Page): Concussion (having signs and symptoms without anatomical lesion) is transient state following a strike to the head.

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: Explain the 'contre-coup' mechanism of brain injury.
back: An injury occurring to the brain on the side opposite the point of impact due to the movement of the brain within the cranial cavity.
citation: Page 90 (Book Page): contre-coup lesion... it has been known to stretch and even rapture brain matter on the opposite side of the impact.

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: Contrast the anatomical locations of Extradural and Subdural hemorrhages.
back:
• Extradural: Between the skull bone and the dura mater.
• Subdural: Between the dura mater and the arachnoid membrane.
citation: Page 90 (Book Page): Extradural hemorrhage... between skull and dura. Subdural hemorrhage... between dura and arachnoid.

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: What characterizes a 'Jaifah' injury under Pakistani law?
back: A 'Hurt' (injury) that extends into the body cavity of the trunk, specifically involving the chest or abdomen.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): Jaifah: Hurt extending to the body cavity of the trunk.

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: What is the mechanism of rapid death in manual strangulation (throttling)?
back: Reflex cardiac asystole caused by stimulation of the vagus nerve or carotid sinus (vagal inhibition).
citation: Page 154 (Book Page): Throttling... Reflex cardiac arrest through Vagus nerve... stimulation of the carotid sinus/vagus nerve.

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: Define the 'Pugilistic Attitude' observed in severe burn victims.
back: A specific boxer-like posture assumed by a corpse due to heat-induced coagulation and shortening of flexor muscle proteins.
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): pugilistic attitude due to heat coagulation and shortening of flexor muscle proteins.

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: Differentiate the ligature mark of hanging from that of strangulation.
back:
• Hanging: Oblique mark, directed upward toward the knot, usually in-continuous.
• Strangulation: Horizontal, continuous mark of uniform depth.
citation: Page 152 (Book Page): Hanging... oblique going upward towards the knot. Page 153 (Book Page): Strangulation... directed transversely across it... Horizontal.

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: What are the specific internal neck findings in a case of throttling?
back:
• Bruising of neck soft tissues (muscles, fascia).
• Fracture of the hyoid bone (usually) and thyroid cartilage (occasionally).
citation: Page 154 (Book Page): Bruises due to pressure of finger-tips... Page 155 (Book Page): Hyoid bone usually and thyroid cartilage occasionally is fractured.

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: Describe the physiological hallmark of traumatic asphyxia (chest compression).
back: Anoxic anoxia resulting from mechanical immobilization of the chest, leading to acute facial congestion, cyanosis, and sub-conjunctival hemorrhages.
citation: Page 156 (Book Page): Traumatic asphyxia is immobilization of chest... Mechanism of death is anoxic anoxia. Autopsy findings are acute congestion of the face, conjunctivae.

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: List the four components of a firearm 'wound-complex'.
back:
1. Entry wound.
2. Trajectory/Track.
3. Bullet resting place.
4. Exit wound.
citation: Page 70 (Book Page): Firearm wound-complex... has four parts: Entry wound, Trajectory with direction, Bullet resting place, Exit Wound.

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: What are the four primary types of intracranial hemorrhages seen in head injuries?
back:
- Extradural hemorrhage
- Subdural hemorrhage
- Subarachnoid hemorrhage
- Intra-cerebral hemorrhage
citation: Page 90 (Book Page): [Important sites of intra-cranial hemorrhages are: Extradural hemorrhage, Subdural hemorrhage, Subarachnoid hemorrhage, Intra-cerebral hemorrhages]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: Describe the pathophysiological mechanism of a 'split' laceration on the scalp.
back:
- Occurs where skin is firmly supported by bone
- Sudden compression between weapon and bone splits tissue
- Often resembles an incised wound
citation: Page 60 (Book Page): [Split laceration occurs on scalp, forehead, chin or any other part of the body where skin is firmly supported by underlying bone. Sudden compression of the skin and other tissues betweenn the weapon and the underlying bone split them.]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: Contrast the effects of head trauma when the head is stationary versus in motion.
back:
- Stationary: Local scalp injury at contact site
- In Motion: Diffuse brain damage (contre-coup) on the opposite side of impact
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [A strike to a stationary head will produce a local injury of the scalp at the site of contact... When a moving head strikes a stationary object, the resultant trauma to the head is usually at the opposite side of strike called contre-coup.]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: Identify the diagnosis for a neck injury with a horizontal, continuous, uniform ligature mark.
back:
- Diagnosis: Homicidal Strangulation
- Differentiated from hanging by its transverse direction and continuity all around the neck
citation: Page 153 (Book Page): [strangulation... ligature mark... directed transversely across it... horizontal and continuous ligature mark of uniform depth all around neck.]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: What physiological event occurs when the carotid sinus is stimulated during neck compression?
back:
- Parasympathetic stimulation of the vagus nerve
- Causes reflex cardiac arrest (asystole)
- Results in rapid death
citation: Page 154 (Book Page): [Pressure on carotid sinus Stimulates vagus nerve precipitating cardiac arrest... increased tension... produces inhibitory circulatory effects such as slowing of pulse]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: List the diagnostic criteria for general pathological changes in asphyxial deaths.
back:
- Generalized cyanosis
- Vascular congestion and edema
- Petechial hemorrhages (Tardieu’s spots)
- Fluidity of blood
citation: Page 149 (Book Page): [Table 13.1: General pathological changes in asphyxia: Generalized cyanosis, Vascular congestion, Edema of the tissues and viscera, Petechial hemorrhages in the skin and viscera, Fluidity of blood]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: Explain the Rowbotham mechanism regarding comminuted depressed fractures of the skull.
back:
- Local force creates a shallow cone
- Inner table at apex fractures first under tension
- Outer table at periphery fractures subsequently
citation: Page 61 (Book Page): [Sequence of events at the site of impact is formation of a shallow cone. Apex of cone stretches the inner-table and compresses the outer table... extension of the break both... results in a comminuted depressed fracture.]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: Differentiate between organic and psychogenic amnesia following head trauma.
back:
- Organic: From brain pathology/trauma; impairs registration and retention
- Psychogenic: From psychological stress; purely an interference in recall
citation: Page 89 (Book Page): [Organic amnesia results from pathological changes in the brain... impairs both registration and retention. Psychogenic amnesia... occurs in situations of psychological stress... interference in the process of recall.]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: What are the primary effects of penetrating wounds to the abdomen?
back:
- Acute hemorrhagic shock from internal vessel/organ damage
- Bulging of intestines (evisceration) through the wound
citation: Page 60 (Book Page): [In penetration of... abdomen... signs of acute hemorrhagic shock due to hemorrhage. Photo 6.15: Penetrating wound abdomen with bulging out intestines]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: Define the 'Greenstick Fracture' observed in childhood limb injuries.
back:
- Occurs in elastic bones of children
- Damage is localized to only one side of the bone
- Caused by force applied to the point of maximum convexity
citation: Page 60 (Book Page): [Long bones of children are comparatively more elastic and show less damage to only one side of bone close to application of force resulting in green stick — fracture.]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: What are the two primary mechanisms of skull fracturing according to Rowbotham?
back:
1. Local deformation (crushing of outer table/bending at site).
2. General deformation (compression of the skull in one plane causing bulging and fracturing in another).
citation: Page 61 (Book Page): [Rowhbotham divides mechanism of fracturing of skull into; local deformation at the site and general deformation of the whole skull.]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: Define the pathophysiological hallmark of cerebral concussion.
back: Transient cerebral dysfunction without anatomical lesion, usually resulting from a head strike and causing a brief period of loss of consciousness.
citation: Page 89 (Book Page): [Concussion (having no anatomical lesion) is transient cerebral dysfunction following a strike to the head... results in a short period of loss of consciousness.]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: Distinguish between the anatomical locations of Extradural and Subdural hemorrhages.
back:
• Extradural: Between the skull bone and the dura mater (often temporal fossa).
• Subdural: Between the dura mater and the arachnoid membrane.
citation: Page 90 (Book Page)-91: [Extradural hemorrhage... most common site of extradural hemorrhage is temporal fossa... Subdural hemorrhage... located between the dura-mater and the arachnoid.]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: A victim of heavy chest compression presents with facial cyanosis and petechiae. Diagnosis?
back: Traumatic Asphyxia. Key features include acute facial congestion, conjunctival hemorrhages, and a clear demarcation line between the compressed and uncompressed areas.
citation: Page 155 (Book Page): [Autopsy findings are acute congestion of the face, conjunctivae and skin of the chest showing a clear demarcation betweenn areas above the level of pressure and one below.]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: Describe the physiological response to increased tension on the carotid sinus during throttling.
back: Stimulates parasympathetic nerves (vagus), causing inhibitory effects: bradycardia, depressed myocardial contractility, and generalized vasodilation (reflex cardiac arrest).
citation: Page 154 (Book Page): [Increased tension... precipitates strong parasympathetic stimulation and produces inhibitory circulatory effects such as slowing of pulse, depression of myocardial contractility.]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: What are the diagnostic hallmarks of a penetrating abdominal wound?
back:
1. Depth is the greatest dimension.
2. Potential evisceration (bulging intestines).
3. Signs of acute hemorrhagic shock.
citation: Page 59 (Book Page): [Penetrating & puncturing wound... depth, which is the greatest dimension... Penetrating wound abdomen with bulging out intestines.]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: What systemic complications typically follow grinding compression injuries to the limbs?
back:
• Precipitation of fat embolism.
• Release of myoglobin (crush syndrome) leading to renal failure.
• Severe hemorrhagic shock.
citation: Page 58 (Book Page): [When grinding compression laceration occurs over wide area, they precipitate fat embolism... causing death from renal failure.]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: Contrast Retrograde versus Anterograde post-traumatic amnesia.
back:
• Retrograde: Memory loss for events occurring BEFORE the injury.
• Anterograde: Memory loss for events occurring AFTER the injury.
citation: Page 89 (Book Page): [Post-traumatic amnesia is of two types: Antrograde amnesia extending forwards from the time of injury... Retrograde amnesia extending backwards from the time of regaining of consciousness.]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: Explain the mechanism of death in pulmonary embolism following lower limb injury.
back: Deep vein thrombosis (DVT) develops in the legs; detached emboli travel via the heart to occlude the main pulmonary artery.
citation: Page 84 (Book Page): [Pulmonary embolism... occurs following development of deep vein thrombosis especially of legs from where an embolus gets detached and cause death.]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: Which specific neck structures are most prone to fracture during throttling?
back:
• Greater cornua of the hyoid bone.
• Superior horn of the thyroid cartilage (especially in elderly/calcified subjects).
citation: Page 150 (Book Page): [Common sites of fractures are greater cornue of hyoid bone and superior horn of thyroid cartilage especially when calcified as in advanced age.]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: What are the four primary types of intracranial hemorrhages resulting from head trauma?
back:
- Extradural hemorrhage
- Subdural hemorrhage
- Subarachnoid hemorrhage
- Intra-cerebral hemorrhage
citation: Page 90 (Book Page): [Important sites of intra-cranial hemorrhages are: Extradural hemorrhage, Subdural hemorrhage, Subarachnoid hemorrhage, Intra-cerebral hemorrhages]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: Describe the physiological mechanism of death from pressure on the carotid sinus during neck compression.
back:
- Stimulation of the carotid sinus or vagus nerve
- Triggers strong parasympathetic (vagal) discharge
- Results in reflex cardiac inhibition and sudden arrest.
citation: Page 154 (Book Page): [v. Carotid - sinus/vagus . nerve, which gets stimulated and precipitates reflex cardiac arrest,]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: Contrast the typical bleeding sources for extradural and subdural intracranial hemorrhages.
back:
- Extradural: Usually arterial (middle meningeal vessels) associated with skull fractures.
- Subdural: Usually venous (perforating or bridging veins) from tearing/shearing.
citation: Page 90 (Book Page)-91: [A depressed fracture... or a linear fracture across middle meningeal artery or vein ruptures them... Subdural hemorrhage... due to slow leakage from a perforating vein.]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: A victim of industrial crushing develops renal failure. Identify the syndrome and renal findings.
back:
- Crush Syndrome
- Renal tubules show swelling, necrosis, and myoglobin/granular casts
- Results from muscle ischemia rather than mechanical obstruction.
citation: Page 84 (Book Page): [Crush syndrome... Pigments like myoglobin and granular casts are seen in the tubules of kidney. This is associated with swelling and necrosis of epithelium and eventual renal failure.]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: Describe the mechanism of fat embolism following trauma to the limbs.
back:
- Mechanical trauma to long bones/adipose tissue releases fat droplets.
- Droplets enter systemic circulation via broken veins.
- Leads to occlusion of pulmonary or systemic capillaries.
citation: Page 84 (Book Page): [Fat embolism follows trauma to the body, more so in crushing injuries of the limbs especially when associated with fractures... releasing fat droplets in the systemic circulation.]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: What are the diagnostic criteria for fatal cardiac tamponade in penetrating chest injuries?
back:
- Accumulation of 10-15 oz. of blood in the pericardial sac.
- Mechanical interference with heart function.
- Results in rapid death.
citation: Page 83 (Book Page): [Effusion of about 10-15 oz. of blood into the pericardial sac will prove fatal due to cardiac tamponade]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: Explain the application of the "Contre-coup" concept in mobile head injuries.
back:
- Injury occurs on the side opposite the site of impact.
- Caused by the brain moving within the skull due to inertia.
- Common in falls or blows to a moving head.
citation: Page 90 (Book Page): [Effects on the brain are immediate... Site of coup injury is where force has been applied... contre-coup injury occurs on the opposite side...]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: Differentiate traumatic from spontaneous intracerebral hemorrhage by typical anatomical location.
back:
- Traumatic: Typically in frontal and temporal white matter.
- Spontaneous: Usually in the basal ganglion regions (hypertensive patients).
citation: Page 92 (Book Page): [Location of post-traumatic hemorrhage is usually in white matter of frontal and temporal regions... Spontaneous hemorrhage is usually in the ganglion regions]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: Describe the physiological loop involved in death from traumatic asphyxia.
back:
- Mechanical immobilization of the chest/abdomen.
- Prevents respiratory excursion and expansion.
- Results in rapid anoxic anoxia and acute facial congestion.
citation: Page 155 (Book Page): [Traumatic asphyxia is immobilization of chest... prevents respiratory movement... results in anoxic anoxia.]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: Which anatomical structures of the neck are most frequently fractured during throttling?
back:
- Greater cornua of the hyoid bone.
- Superior horns of the thyroid cartilage (especially if calcified).
citation: Page 150 (Book Page): [Common sites of fracture are greater cornue of hyoid bone and superior horn of thyroid cartilage especially when calcified]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: What is the classic clinical definition of a 'black eye' in forensic trauma?
back: A result of gravity shifting of blood from an injury on the forehead or scalp to the lax periorbital tissue.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [Gravity shifting of bruise occurs from its initial site along tissue line of least resistance to below region under the influence of gravity... later causing black eye.]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: Describe the mechanism of renal failure in 'Crush Syndrome' following limb injury.
back:
- Release of myoglobin from damaged muscles.
- Myoglobin and granular casts obstruct renal tubules.
- Renal ischemia leads to failure.
citation: Page 84 (Book Page): [Pigments like myoglobin and granular casts are seen in the tubules of kidney... eventual renal failure. It was suggested that it is due to attempt on the part of kidney to excrete acid metabolites from damaged muscles.]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: Contrast the presentation of post-traumatic versus spontaneous intracerebral hemorrhage.
back:
- Post-traumatic: White matter (frontal/temporal); healthy individuals.
- Spontaneous: Basal ganglia; associated with hypertension and aneurysms.
citation: Page 92 (Book Page): [Location of post-traumatic hemorrhage is usually in the white matter of frontal and temporal regions... Spontaneous hemorrhage is usually in the ganglion regions in a patient who is overweight and has a history of high blood pressure.]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: Identify the most likely injury for a victim presenting with a 'lucid interval' after temporal trauma.
back:
- Extradural Hemorrhage.
- Usually caused by rupture of the middle meningeal vessels.
citation: Page 90 (Book Page): [The most common site of extradural hemorrhage is temporal fossa due to the rupture of middle meningeal vessels... posterior fossa hemorrhage may not be immediately fatal.]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: What are the three primary mechanisms of death in mechanical constriction of the neck?
back:
- Cerebral anoxia (vessel compression).
- Asphyxia (airway obstruction).
- Vagal inhibition (reflex cardiac arrest from carotid sinus pressure).
citation: Page 152 (Book Page): [Mechanism of death in hanging includes... cerebral anoxia, reflex cardiac arrest and pure asphyxia.]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: List the four classic autopsy findings associated with fatal asphyxia.
back:
- Generalized cyanosis.
- Vascular congestion.
- Petechial hemorrhages (Tardieu's spots).
- Visceral edema and fluidity of blood.
citation: Page 149 (Book Page): [Table 13.1: General pathological changes in asphyxia: Generalized cyanosis, Vascular congestion, Edema of the tissues and viscera, Petechial hemorrhages in the skin and viscera, Fluidity of blood.]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: How is 'pneumothorax' demonstrated during a forensic autopsy?
back: Form a pocket in chest muscle with water and stab an intercostal space under the water to observe escaping air bubbles.
citation: Page 120 (Book Page): [Thorax may be opened after testing... presence of pneumo-thorax... An intercostals space is stabbed with a scalpel below the water level to note the escape of air bubbles.]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: Differentiate suicidal from homicidal cutthroat wounds based on 'tailing' and hesitation cuts.
back:
- Suicidal: Hesitation cuts and 'tailing' present.
- Homicidal: Hesitation cuts and 'tailing' absent; wound deep/bold in center.
citation: Page 80 (Book Page): [Table 7.5: Suicidal... Hesitation cut: Near initiation point... Tailing: Present on working hand side. Homicidal... Hesitation cut: Absent... Tailing: Absent.]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: Describe the 'Vago-vagal inhibition' mechanism triggered by neck pressure.
back:
- Stimulation of carotid sinus or vagus nerve.
- Intense parasympathetic discharge.
- Precipitates sudden cardiac arrest and circulatory failure.
citation: Page 154 (Book Page): [Sudden sympatho-adrenal or parasympathetic stimulation leads to circulatory failure... Vagus nerve... Carotid sinus... Reflex cardiac arrest through Vagus nerve.]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: Which bone is most commonly fractured in manual strangulation (throttling)?
back: The Hyoid bone (greater cornua).
citation: Page 153 (Book Page): [Hyoid bone usually and thyroid cartilage occasionally is fractured.]

category: Explain mechanism of injuries to soft and bony tissues of head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: Which two factors of a weapon determine the kinetic energy applied to tissues during a mechanical strike?
back:
- Weight of the weapon
- Velocity of the weapon ($KE = 1/2mv^2$)
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [Weight and velocity of weapon and their sum-total control and determine appearance of the wound. Velocity has kinetic energy, which is calculated by formula, K.E.=1/2mv^2.]

category: Explain mechanism of injuries to soft and bony tissues of head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: What is the pathophysiological mechanism responsible for the formation of a bruise (contusion)?
back:
- Sudden tissue indentation followed by recoil
- Rupture of small blood vessels (capillaries)
- Extravasation of blood into the surrounding interstitial tissue
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [results from sudden tissue indentation followed by recoil... blood from the broken blow vessels spread into the surrounding tissue.]

category: Explain mechanism of injuries to soft and bony tissues of head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: Contrast the mechanical causes of split (crush) lacerations versus over-stretch lacerations.
back:
- Split: Skin is compressed/crushed between the weapon and underlying bone.
- Over-stretch: Pressure combined with a push pulls skin away from its underlying attachments.
citation: Page 57 (Book Page)-58: [Split... Sudden compression of the skin and other tissues between the weapon and the underlying bone split them... Over-stretch... Pressure along with push on the skin... pull it from the underlying tissue.]

category: Explain mechanism of injuries to soft and bony tissues of head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: Explain Rowbotham’s mechanism of local deformation in skull fractures.
back:
- Impact creates a shallow cone.
- Apex of cone stretches the inner table.
- Periphery of cone compresses the outer table.
- Fracture occurs if distortion exceeds bone strength.
citation: Page 61 (Book Page): [Sequence of events at the site of impact is formation of a shallow cone. Apex of cone stretches the inner-table and compresses the outer table... distortion is beyond the strength of the bone, a fracture... results.]

category: Explain mechanism of injuries to soft and bony tissues of head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: What physiological step leads to reflex cardiac arrest during mechanical neck compression?
back:
- Mechanical stimulation of the carotid sinus or vagus nerve
- Parasympathetic/inhibitory discharge
- Results in slowing of pulse and sudden cardiac asystole
citation: Page 154 (Book Page): [Reflex cardiac asystole takes place due to variations of tension within carotid sinuses... Increased tension... produces inhibitory circulatory effects such as slowing of pulse... and sudden arrest.]

category: Explain mechanism of injuries to soft and bony tissues of head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: List the four components that must be analyzed in a firearm 'wound-complex'.
back:
1. Entry wound
2. Trajectory and direction
3. Projectile resting place
4. Exit wound
citation: Page 70 (Book Page): [Firearm wound-complex is name allocated to some-total resultant damage findings of fire-blast on target. It has four parts: Entry wound; Trajectory with direction; Bullet resting place; Exit Wound.]

category: Explain mechanism of injuries to soft and bony tissues of head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: Explain the mechanism by which a high-velocity bullet causes damage larger than its own diameter.
back:
- Creation of temporary cavitation via radial energy dissipation
- Instant lateral displacement of soft tissues
- Permanent cavity remains after tissue recoil/collapse
citation: Page 69 (Book Page): [High velocity bullet... additionally produces a temporary cavitation in soft tissues... creating instant cavitation... leaving a permanent cavity or damage, which is larger than the diameter of low velocity bullet.]

category: Explain mechanism of injuries to soft and bony tissues of head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: Differentiate between Coup and Contre-coup mechanisms of intracranial injury.
back:
- Coup: Damage at the primary site of impact.
- Contre-coup: Damage at the opposite side of the brain due to inertia and skull partitions.
citation: Page 89 (Book Page)-90: [Lesions may be cither coup or contre-coup... Site of coup injury is where force has been applied... contre-coup... at the opposite side... because of many partitions of cranial cavity.]

category: Explain mechanism of injuries to soft and bony tissues of head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: Describe the physiological loop characterizing Phase II (Struggle Phase) of fatal asphyxia.
back:
- Expiratory struggle
- Deepening cyanosis
- Engorgement of neck veins
- Development of Tardieu’s spots (petechial hemorrhages)
citation: Page 149 (Book Page): [Phase II is characterized by struggle to breathe... Cyanosis deepens with engorgement of neck veins. Generalized congestion and petechial hemorrhages start appearing.]

category: Explain mechanism of injuries to soft and bony tissues of head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: Which anatomic structures in the body act as the primary conductors of electrical current?
back:
- Nerves
- Blood fluid
- These offer the least resistance, unlike skin which generates heat when resisting current.
citation: Page 65 (Book Page): [Nerve and blood fluid offer almost no resistance and act as good conductor... skin relatively provides the resistance and generates heat causing thermal lesion.]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: Define the transient clinical state of "concussion" following a strike to the head.
back:
- Transient loss of consciousness following a strike.
- Absence of any gross anatomical lesion.
- May occur following a strike to a stationary or mobile head.
citation: Page 89 (Book Page): [Concussion (having no anatomical lesion) is transient following a strike to the head... loss of consciousness... there are no positive findings in EEG and autopsy]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: Explain the "Coup" versus "Contre-coup" mechanism in cerebral contusion injuries.
back:
- Coup: Lesion located at the site of impact.
- Contre-coup: Lesion located diametrically opposite the site of impact.
- Caused by stretching of brain matter during trauma.
citation: Page 90 (Book Page): [Coup lesion is at the site of impact whereas contre-coup is diametrically opposite... stretch and pull the brain matter]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: Contrast the anatomical source of bleeding in Extradural versus Subdural hemorrhages.
back:
- Extradural: Rupture of middle meningeal artery/vein (associated with skull fracture).
- Subdural: Rupture of superior cerebral vein at its entry to the sagittal sinus.
citation: Page 90 (Book Page), 91: [Extradural... rupture of the middle meningeal artery or vein... Subdural... rupture of a superior cerebral vein at the point of its entry into the sagittal sinus]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: Identify the typical anatomical sites of "Primary Impact" injuries in a pedestrian-vehicle collision.
back:
- Located on legs, thighs, or hips.
- Distribution corresponds to the height of the vehicle's bumper.
- Often involves fractures and localized bruising.
citation: Page 87 (Book Page): [Primary impact injuries are situated on legs, thighs or hips... distribution of these injuries to different surfaces of the body... depends upon whether impact is primary]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: Describe the physiological consequence of mechanical pressure applied to the "Carotid Sinus" in the neck.
back:
- Stimulates the vagus nerve (parasympathetic response).
- Leads to reflex cardiac inhibition or arrest.
- Results in sudden death without typical asphyxial signs.
citation: Page 150 (Book Page), 154: [Pressure on carotid sinus... Stimulates vagus nerve precipitating cardiac arrest... inhibitory circulatory effects such as slowing of pulse]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: What are the two characteristic fracture sites in the neck during manual strangulation?
back:
- Greater cornua of the hyoid bone.
- Superior horn of the thyroid cartilage.
- Common in advanced age due to calcification.
citation: Page 150 (Book Page): [Common sites of fractures are greater cornue of hyoid bone and superior horn of thyroid cartilage especially when they are calcified]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: List the external clinical hallmarks of "Traumatic Asphyxia" caused by chest immobilization.
back:
- Acute congestion and cyanosis of the face and neck.
- Sub-conjunctival hemorrhages.
- Clear demarcation line between compressed and non-compressed areas.
citation: Page 155 (Book Page): [Acute congestion of the face, conjunctivae and skin of the chest showing a clear demarcation betweenn areas above the level of pressure]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: Differentiate a "Split Laceration" on the scalp from an "Incised Wound."
back:
- Split Laceration: Irregular margins, bridging tissue tags, and crushed hair bulbs.
- Incised Wound: Clean-cut margins, sharp angles, and hair cut cleanly.
citation: Page 57 (Book Page), 59: [Split laceration... resembling an incision wound... bridging tissue tags and hair... forced into the wound... Incised wound... clean cut margins, sharp angles and smooth walls]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: What is the physiological consequence of "Grinding Compression" injuries to the limbs?
back:
- Separation of skin and muscles from underlying bone (flaying).
- Extravasation of blood into crushed tissues.
- Precipitation of fatal fat embolism or renal failure.
citation: Page 58 (Book Page), 84: [Grinding compression... skin and muscles are also separated... precipitate fat embolism... causing death from renal failure]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: Why are "Greenstick" fractures common in children following limb trauma?
back:
- Children's bones are highly elastic.
- Impact causes bone to bend and break only on one side (the side opposite the force).
citation: Page 60 (Book Page): [Long bones of children are comparatively more elastic and show less damage to only one side of bone... green stick fracture]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: What are the three types of blunt force lacerations categorized by mechanism?
back:
1. Split (crush) laceration
2. Over-stretch laceration
3. Grinding compression laceration
citation: Page 60 (Book Page): [Lacerated wound is an open wound... Depending upon mechanism of its causation, there are of three types: Split, also called crush laceration, Over-stretch laceration, Grinding compression laceration]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: Describe the mechanism of a 'black eye' resulting from a forehead injury.
back: Gravity shifts extravasated blood from the forehead along tissue lines of least resistance into the lax orbital tissues within 24 hours.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [Gravity shifting of bruise occurs from its initial site along tissue line of least resistance to below region under the influence of gravity within first 24 hours. It changes both its position and shape as noticed following a blow on the forehead/scalp and later causing black eye]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: Differentiate the appearance of rifled bullet entry wounds versus shotgun pellet entries.
back: Rifled bullet: Single circular hole with inverted margins. Shotgun: Multiple 'peppering' holes (in far range) or en-mass entry (in contact range).
citation: Page 71 (Book Page): [Riffled weapon entry wound is typically circular hole with inverted margins... Page 74 (Book Page): Entry wound shotgun differs from rifled wound... shotgun many holes depending upon distance of fire]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: A victim presents with a horizontal, continuous neck groove and intense cyanosis. Name the likely manner of death.
back: Homicidal strangulation. The horizontal direction and intense facial congestion differentiate it from the oblique, non-continuous mark of hanging.
citation: Page 153 (Book Page): [In strangulation... directed transversely across it... Table 13.3: Direction: Horizontal. Cyanosis: Intense. Facial congestion: Marked]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: What is the critical pharmacological step in managing acute organo-phosphate poisoning?
back: Administer 2 mg Atropine sulfate IV as a test dose, repeating frequently until pulmonary secretions cease.
citation: Page 170 (Book Page): [In the case of organo-phosphate poisoning, a test dose of 2 mg intravenously should be administered... dosage of atropine sulfate must be increased and repeated frequently until cessation of secretion]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: List the four primary anatomical sites for internal traumatic hemorrhages within the head.
back:
1. Extradural
2. Subdural
3. Subarachnoid
4. Intracerebral
citation: Page 90 (Book Page): [Important sites of intra-cranial hemorrhages are: Extradural hemorrhage, Subdural hemorrhage, Subarachnoid hemorrhage, Intra-cerebral hemorrhages]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
coreConcept: Rule of Nine for Body Surface Area
front: Q: Apply the 'Rule of Nine' to calculate the surface area of a single burnt lower limb.
back: The front of one thigh, leg, and foot is 9%, and the back is 9%, totaling 18% per lower limb.
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [Table 6.7: Front of thigh, leg & foot of right side 9%; Back of thigh, leg & sole of foot of right side 9%]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: Distinguish post-mortem skin splits from ante-mortem lacerations in burn cases.
back: Post-mortem splits lack vital reaction (hyperemia/inflammation) and occur due to heat-induced protein coagulation and tissue shrinkage.
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [Postmortem artifact which are produced by fire... skin splits... Area showing pseudo-bruising lacks vital reaction]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: Why does asphyxia lead to generalized cyanosis of the face and neck?
back: Anoxia causes capillo-venous engorgement and a terminal rise in reduced hemoglobin/carbon dioxide in circulating blood.
citation: Page 149 (Book Page): [Capillo-venous engorgement with rise in the level of carbon dioxide in circulating blood produces generalized congestion and cyanosis]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: Name the specific neck bones/cartilages most frequently fractured in manual throttling.
back: Greater cornua of the hyoid bone or the superior horn of the thyroid cartilage.
citation: Page 150 (Book Page): [Common sites of fracture are greater cornue of hyoid bone and superior horn of thyroid cartilage especially when calcified]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: Define the anatomical location and primary cause of an extradural hemorrhage in head injuries.
back:
• Location: Between the skull bone and the duramater.
• Cause: Usually exclusively traumatic, involving a fracture that ruptures the middle meningeal vessels in the temporal fossa.
citation: Page 90 (Book Page): [Extradural hemorrhage in adults is exclusively traumatic... rupture them to cause hemorrhage. The most common site of extradural hemorrhage is temporal fossa due to the rupture of middle meningeal vessels.]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: Describe the pathophysiological mechanism and defining feature of a cerebral concussion.
back:
• Mechanism: Transient paralysis of brain function caused by a blow or fall.
• Feature: No visible anatomical lesion is present upon autopsy or EEG.
citation: Page 89 (Book Page): [Concussion (having no anatomical lesion) is transient paralysis of brain function following a strike to the head.]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: Contrast the orientation and continuity of ligature marks in hanging versus strangulation.
back:
• Hanging: Oblique, non-continuous (absent at knot), situated high in the neck.
• Strangulation: Horizontal, continuous (all around), situated lower (middle of neck).
citation: Page 153 (Book Page): [Hanging: Oblique, Incomplete... High up in the neck. Strangulation: Horizontal, Complete... Middle of neck.]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: A victim presents with memory loss for events occurring *after* a head impact. Identify this condition.
back:
• Anterograde Amnesia.
• It involves memory loss extending forwards from the time of injury, as opposed to retrograde which extends backwards.
citation: Page 89 (Book Page): [Antrograde amnesia extending forwards from the time of injury; Retrograde amnesia extending backwards from the time of regaining of consciousness.]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: Explain the mechanism behind a "greenstick" fracture in pediatric limb injuries.
back:
• Elasticity: Children's bones are more elastic than adults.
• Action: The bone bends under force and breaks only on one side close to the point of impact.
citation: Page 60 (Book Page): [Long bones of children are comparatively more elastic and show less damage to only on side of bone close to application of force resulting in green stick — fracture.]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: Identify the common skeletal structures fractured during manual throttling (manual strangulation).
back:
• Greater cornue of the hyoid bone.
• Superior horn of the thyroid cartilage (especially in older cases where it is calcified).
citation: Page 150 (Book Page): [Common sites of fractures are greater cornue of hyoid bone and superior horn of thyroid cartilage especially when calcified as in advanced age.]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: Describe the autopsy procedure used to confirm the presence of a pneumothorax in chest trauma.
back:
• Create a pocket between the skin and ribs.
• Fill with water and stab an intercostal space.
• Observe for escaping air bubbles replacing the water.
citation: Page 120 (Book Page): [An inverted graduated glass cylinder is held in the pocket containing water and the thorax is stabbed with a scalpel... show gas bubbles replacing the water.]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: Contrast the reaction of a high-velocity bullet striking solid organs versus fluid-filled hollow viscera.
back:
• Solid (Liver): Disintegrates and disorganizes large areas.
• Hollow (Stomach/Heart): Displaces fluid explosively in all directions, creating secondary projectiles and massive cavitation.
citation: Page 70 (Book Page): [When a hollow viscus containing fluid is hit by a high velocity bullet, its contents get separated into particles, which get displaced explosively in all directions away from the bullet path and behave as secondary projectiles.]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: Explain the physiological result of increased tension on the carotid sinus during neck compression.
back:
• Strong parasympathetic stimulation.
• Causes slowing of the pulse and depression of myocardial conductivity, leading to reflex cardiac arrest.
citation: Page 154 (Book Page): [Increased tension... Precipitates strong parasympathetic stimulation and produces inhibitory circulatory effects such as slowing of pulse... reflex cardiac asystole.]

category: Describe effects of injuries to head, neck, chest, abdomen and limbs
front: Q: List the clinical hallmarks of a "Grinding Compression" injury to the limbs.
back:
• Multiple skin tears.
• Degloving (separation of skin and subcutaneous tissue from underlying muscle).
• Deep extravasations of crushed tissue.
citation: Page 58 (Book Page): [Characteristics of such a wound are multiple skin tears; skin and subcutaneous tissues are also separated from the underlying muscles and other tissues.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: Define 'Hurt' under the Qisas and Diyat Ordinance.
back: Causing pain, harm, disease, infirmity, or injury. Impairing, disabling, or dismembering any organ or part without causing death.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): [Hurt is defined as and means causing of pain, harm, disease, infirmity, injury or impairing, disabling, dismembering any organ of the body or part thereof withoutt causing death.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: What is the specific sequence of local deformation in a skull fracture?
back: Shallow cone forms at impact. Apex stretches the inner table (fracturing it first). Periphery convexity is directed outwards, compressing the outer table.
citation: Page 61 (Book Page): [Sequence of events ai the site of impact is formation of a shallow cone. ‘Apex of cone stretches the inner-table and compresses the ‘outer table... inner-table at the apex of the cone fractures belore the outer table]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: Distinguish between Itlaf-i-udw and Itlaf-i-salahiyyat-i-udw.
back: Itlaf-i-udw: Dismemberment, amputation, or severing of a limb/organ. Itlaf-i-salahiyyat-i-udw: Destroying or permanently impairing the function/capacity of an organ or causing permanent disfigurement.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): [Itlaf-i-udw Causing of dismemberment, amputation, severcment of any limb or organ... Itlaf-i-Salahiyyat-i-Udw Destroying of permanently impairing the function or capacity of an organ or causing permanent disfigurement]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: Differentiate post-traumatic from spontaneous intracerebral hemorrhage.
back: Traumatic: usually in white matter of frontal/temporal lobes; symptoms onset ~1 week. Spontaneous: usually in basal ganglia; associated with overweight, hypertension, or aneurysms.
citation: Page 92 (Book Page): [Location of post-traumatic hemorrhage is usually in white matter of frontal and temporal regions... Spontaneous hemorrhage is usually in the ganglion regions in a patient who is overweight and has a history of high blood pressure]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: What is the mechanism of reflex cardiac arrest in manual neck compression?
back: Variation in tension of carotid sinus or vagus nerve stimulation. Triggers strong parasympathetic/inhibitory circulatory effects, leading to pulse slowing and sudden arrest.
citation: Page 154 (Book Page): [Reflex cardiac asystole takes place dure to variations of tension within carotid sinuses... increased tension... precipitates strong parasympathetic stimulation and produces inhibitory circulatory effects]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: Define the diagnostic criteria for Shajjah-i-Mudihah.
back: A hurt on the head or face characterized by the exposing of bone without its fracture.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): [Shajjah-i-Mudihah Exposing of bone withoutt its fracture.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: Define a 'Jaifah' injury in the context of regional trauma.
back: Any hurt where the injury extends into the body cavity of the trunk (thorax or abdomen).
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): [Jaifah Hurt extending to the body cavity of the trunk.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: Contrast the site and source of Extradural versus Subdural hemorrhages.
back: Extradural: temporal fossa; source is middle meningeal vessels. Subdural: surface of cerebral hemisphere; source is communicating or perforating veins.
citation: Page 90 (Book Page)-91: [Extradural hemorrhage... temporal fossa due to the rupture of middle meningeal vessels... Subdural hemorrhage... leakage from a perforating vein.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: Explain the mechanism of a 'Contre-coup' brain injury.
back: Accumulation of blood or lesion on the surface of the cerebral hemisphere opposite the point of force application due to brain movement stretching communicating veins.
citation: Page 90 (Book Page)-91: [accumulation of blood on the surface of the cerebral hemisphere on the opposite side with stretching and dislocation of cerebral vein at the site of contre-coup.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: What defines Shajjah-i-Damighah in head injuries?
back: A fracturing of the head/face bones that results in the rupturing of the brain membranes (meninges).
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): [Shajjah-i-Damighah Fracturing of bone with rupturing of the brain membranes.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: Contrast 'Coup' versus 'Contre-coup' brain injuries in regional head trauma.
back:
- Coup: Damage at the actual site of impact.
- Contre-coup: Damage on the opposite side of impact due to brain movement within the cranium.
citation: Page 89 (Book Page): [The coup injury occurs at the site of impact... whereas the injury at the opposite side is called a contre-coup injury.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: What is the pathophysiological mechanism of reflex cardiac arrest in neck compression?
back:
- Mechanical pressure on the carotid sinus or vagus nerve stimulates parasympathetic pathways.
- Results in sudden inhibitory effects, causing immediate cardiac asystole.
citation: Page 150 (Book Page): [Pressure on carotid sinus/vagus nerve, which gets stimulated and precipitates reflex cardiac arrest.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: Differentiate the direction of the ligature mark in hanging versus strangulation.
back:
- Hanging: Oblique, directed upward toward the knot, usually in-continuous.
- Strangulation: Horizontal and transverse across the neck, usually continuous.
citation: Page 153 (Book Page): [Hanging: Oblique... Incomplete... Strangulation: Horizontal... Complete.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: What are the clinical and anatomical hallmarks of Extradural Hemorrhage?
back:
- Exclusively traumatic; involves rupture of middle meningeal vessels.
- Primarily located in the temporal fossa between the skull bone and dura mater.
citation: Page 90 (Book Page): [Extradural hemorrhage in adults is exclusively traumatic... The most common site of extradural hemorrhage is temporal fossa due to the rupture of middle meningeal vessels.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: Define the two types of Post-traumatic Amnesia following head injury.
back:
- Retrograde: Loss of memory for events extending backwards before the injury.
- Anterograde: Memory loss extending forwards from the time of regaining consciousness.
citation: Page 89 (Book Page): [Post-traumatic amnesia is of two types: Antrograde amnesia extending forwards... Retrograde amnesia extending backwards.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: What are the defining diagnostic features of a concussion?
back:
- Transient loss of consciousness following head impact.
- Absence of visible anatomical lesions on gross autopsy or EEG.
citation: Page 89 (Book Page): [Concussion (without an anatomical lesion) is transient period of loss of consciousness following a strike to the head.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: Describe Rowbotham’s 'General Deformation' mechanism for skull fractures.
back:
- Compression in one plane causes the skull to behave like an elastic sphere.
- The skull bulges in the opposite plane, causing fissured fractures distant from impact.
citation: Page 61 (Book Page): [When skull is compressed in one plane, it behaves as an elastic sphere and bulges out in other plane where fracture occurs.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: Differentiate the clinical progression of acute versus latent Subdural Hemorrhage.
back:
- Acute: Symptoms of compression (lethargy, coma) manifest in 24-48 hours.
- Latent: Slow leakage from perforating veins; remains asymptomatic for months as an encapsulated cyst.
citation: Page 91 (Book Page): [In acute variety symptoms of compression manifest in about 24-48 hours... Latent form of subdural hemorrhage develops due to slow leakage from a perforating vein.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: Explain the physiological loop causing death in Traumatic Asphyxia.
back:
- Immobilization of the chest by heavy weight prevents respiratory movements.
- Leads to rapid anoxic anoxia and characteristic acute facial congestion/cyanosis.
citation: Page 155 (Book Page): [Traumatic asphyxia is immobilization of chest... Mechanism of death is anoxic anoxia.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: What specific bone fractures are diagnostic markers of manual strangulation (throttling)?
back:
- Fracture of the greater cornua of the hyoid bone.
- Occasional fracture of the superior horns of the thyroid cartilage.
citation: Page 150 (Book Page): [Common sites of fractures are greater cornue of hyoid bone and superior horn of thyroid cartilage.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: Medicolegally, how is 'hurt' defined under the Qisas & Diyat Ordinance?
back: Causing pain, harm, disease, infirmity, or injury; or impairing, disabling, or dismembering any organ or part of the body without causing death.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): [Hurt is defined as and means causing of pain, harm, disease, infirmity, injury or impairing, disabling, dismembering any organ of the body or part thereof without causing death.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: What is the mechanical mechanism and common site of a 'Split Laceration'?
back: Occurs on scalp, forehead, or chin where skin is firmly supported by bone. Sudden compression between the weapon and bone splits the tissue.
citation: Page 57 (Book Page): [Split, also called crush laceration... occurs on scalp, forehead, chin or any other part of the body where skin is firmly supported by underlying bone. Sudden compression of the skin and other tissues between the weapon and the underlying bone split them.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: How is an antemortem bruise differentiated from postmortem lividity (pseudo-bruising) upon incision?
back: Bruise: Extravasated blood is in interstitial tissue and cannot be washed away. Lividity: Blood is contained within vessels and flows out easily upon cutting.
citation: Page 60 (Book Page): [Table 6.3: Bruise (Anti-mortem) 1. Blood vessels are broken and blood is present in surrounding inter-statius tissue... Pseudo-bruising (Postmortem Lividity) 1. Blood is within the vessels and when incised, blood flows from the mouths of the blood vessel.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: Contrast the injury patterns of a strike to a stationary head versus a moving head hitting a surface.
back: Stationary strike: Localized damage at site of contact. Moving head (deceleration): Widespread trauma, including contrecoup brain injuries opposite the impact site.
citation: Page 53 (Book Page): [A strike to a stationary head will produce a local injury of the scalp at the site of contact... In a fall where the head is in motion and hits a stationary object, the resultant trauma to the head is widespread.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: Describe Rowbotham's sequence for a depressed skull fracture via local deformation.
back: Force forms a shallow cone; the apex stretches and fractures the inner-table first, followed by the outer-table fracturing at the periphery.
citation: Page 61 (Book Page): [Sequence of events at the site of impact is formation of a shallow cone. Apex of cone stretches the inner-table and compresses the outer table... inner-table at the apex of the cone fractures before the outer table.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: What are the defining macroscopic features of an incised wound?
back: Linear or spindle-shaped; clean-cut margins; sharp angles; smooth walls; no tissue bridging; hair bulbs are cut.
citation: Page 59 (Book Page): [Wound is generally linear or spindle shaped... shows clean cut margins, sharp angles and smooth walls. If involved area is hair bearing, it shows cutting of hair including bulbs.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: What is the medicolegal significance of 'Gravity Shifting' in a bruise?
back: Blood moves along tissue lines (e.g., forehead blow causing 'black eye' later). It helps determine the original site of trauma and age of injury.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [Gravity shifting of bruise occurs from its initial site along tissue line of least resistance to below region under the influence of gravity... noticed following a blow on the forehead/scalp and later causing black eye.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: Differentiate traumatic from spontaneous intra-cerebral hemorrhage based on location.
back: Traumatic: Usually located in frontal and temporal white matter. Spontaneous: Primarily occurs in the basal ganglia/ganglion regions of hypertensive patients.
citation: Page 92 (Book Page): [Location of post-traumatic hemorrhage is usually in white matter of frontal and temporal region... Spontaneous hemorrhage is usually in the ganglion regions in a patient... of high blood pressure.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: Explain the mechanism of 'Vagal Inhibition' in sudden death during manual strangulation.
back: External pressure on the carotid sinus or vagus nerve triggers parasympathetic stimulation, causing immediate cardiac arrest/asystole.
citation: Page 154 (Book Page): [Stimulation of carotid sinus/vagus nerve, which gets stimulated and precipitates reflex cardiac arrest... increased tension occurs either by occlusion of the carotid artery above the sinus or by application of pressure on the carotid sinus.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: Which specific laryngeal bones/cartilages are most vulnerable to fracture in manual throttling?
back: Fractures primarily involve the greater cornua of the hyoid bone and the superior horn of the thyroid cartilage.
citation: Page 150 (Book Page): [Common sites of fractures are greater cornue of hyoid bone and superior horn of thyroid cartilage especially when calcified as in advanced age.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: What are the two primary differentiating features between a bruise and postmortem lividity?
