back: 1. Bruise shows vital reaction (swelling/inflammation); Lividity does not. 2. Incised bruise has blood in tissue spaces; Lividity has blood localized within vessels.
citation: Page 57 (Book Page): [Table 13.1: Bruise (Anti-mortem): Blood vessels are broken and blood is present in surrounding tissue... Postmortem lividity: Blood is within the vessels and when incised, can be easily washed with water.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: Explain the medicolegal mechanism of a "black eye" following blunt trauma to the forehead.
back: It represents gravity shifting of effused blood from a forehead injury along tissue lines of least resistance, usually appearing within 24 hours.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [Gravity shifting of bruise occurs from its initial site along tissue line of least resistance... noticed following a blow on the forehead/scalp and later causing black eye.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: Contrast the wound position and depth in suicidal versus homicidal cutthroat injuries.
back: Suicidal: High up in neck, maximum depth at initiation, tailing present. Homicidal: Middle/lower neck, uniform depth throughout, no tailing/hesitation cuts.
citation: Page 80 (Book Page): [Table 7.5: Suicidal: High up... Maximum at the point of initiation... Homicidal: Middle of the neck... Maximum depth in the middle.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: A victim dies rapidly from a neck vein injury. What specific volume of air precipitates fatal air embolism?
back: A volume of approximately 60 ml or more of air introduced into the venous circulation is sufficient to cause immediate death.
citation: Page 83 (Book Page): [Volume of introduced air sufficient to cause death is about 60 ml or more.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: Describe Rowhbotham’s mechanism of "Local Deformation" at the site of skull impact.
back: 1. Shallow cone formation. 2. Apex stretches inner table (fracturing it first). 3. Periphery compresses outer table (fracturing it later).
citation: Page 61 (Book Page): [Sequence of events at the site of impact is formation of a shallow cone. Apex of cone stretches the inner-table... inner-table at the apex of the cone fractures before the outer table.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: What defines the "Pugilistic attitude" in a burned corpse, and is it a vital sign?
back: A postmortem artifact caused by heat-induced protein coagulation and shortening of flexor muscles. It occurs regardless of whether burning was ante-mortem or postmortem.
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [Dead body acquires a specific boxer attitude called pugilistic attitude due to heat coagulation and shortening of flexor muscle proteins... even a dead body will attain it.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: Define the medicolegal term "Hurt" as used in the Qisas and Diyat Ordinance.
back: Causing pain, harm, disease, infirmity, injury or impairing/disabling/dismembering any organ or part of the body without causing death.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): [Hurt is defined as and means causing of pain, harm, disease, infirmity, injury or impairing, disabling, dismembering any organ of the body or part thereof without causing death.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: Differentiate between "Coup" and "Contre-coup" brain injuries in terms of site of impact.
back: Coup: Injury occurs directly at the site of impact. Contre-coup: Injury occurs at the pole diametrically opposite to the site of impact.
citation: Page 90 (Book Page): [Site of coup injury is where force has been applied... contre-coup injury occurs at the pole diametrically opposite to the site of impact.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: What is the physiological mechanism of reflex cardiac asystole during manual strangulation (throttling)?
back: Sudden pressure on the carotid sinus/vagus nerve induces strong parasympathetic stimulation, causing immediate cardiac inhibition and circulatory collapse.
citation: Page 154 (Book Page): [Reflex cardiac asystole takes place due to variations of tension within carotid sinuses... precipitating strong parasympathetic stimulation and produces inhibitory circulatory effects.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: Which skeletal structures of the neck are most commonly fractured during manual strangulation?
back: The greater cornua of the hyoid bone and the superior horn of the thyroid cartilage, particularly in elderly victims.
citation: Page 150 (Book Page): [Common sites are greater cornua of hyoid bone and superior horn of thyroid cartilage especially when calcified as in advanced age.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: Define 'Shajjah' according to the Qisas and Diyat Ordinance.
back:
* Hurt specifically on the head or face.
* Must not amount to Itlaf-i-Udw (dismemberment) or Itlaf-i-Salahiyyat-i-Udw (functional loss).
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): [Hurt on the head or face which does not amount to thaf-i-Udw or itlaf-i-Salahiyyat-i-Udw.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: Explain the mechanism of 'Local Deformation' during skull impact.
back:
* Impact forms a shallow cone.
* The apex of the cone stretches and fractures the inner table before the outer table.
citation: Page 61 (Book Page): [Apex of cone stretches the inner-table and compresses the outer table... inner-table at the apex of the cone fractures before the outer table.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: Differentiate between 'Shajjah-i-Khafifah' and 'Shajjah-i-Mudihah'.
back:
* Khafifah: Hurt without exposing the bone.
* Mudihah: Exposing the bone without resulting in a fracture.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): [Shajjah-i-Khafifah: Hurt withoutt exposing of bone. Shajjah-i-Mudihah: Exposing of bone withoutt its fracture.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: A victim presents with lethargy progressing to coma 24 hours after head trauma. Diagnosis?
back:
* Acute Subdural Hemorrhage.
* Caused by torn communicating cerebral veins, manifesting symptoms within 24-48 hours.
citation: Page 91 (Book Page): [In acute cases symptoms of compression manifest in about 24-48 hours... lethargy increasing to coma.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: Define 'Jaifah' regional injuries of the trunk.
back: * A hurt that extends into the body cavity of the trunk (chest or abdomen).
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): [Jaifah: Hurt extending to the body cavity of the trunk.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: Identify the most common regional site and vascular source for Extradural Hemorrhage.
back:
* Site: Temporal fossa.
* Source: Rupture of the middle meningeal artery or vein, usually due to a linear fracture.
citation: Page 90 (Book Page): [most common site of extradural hemorrhage is temporal fossa due to the rupture of middle meningeal vessels.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: Contrast 'Coup' and 'Contre-coup' brain lesions in regional head trauma.
back:
* Coup: Injury occurs at the direct site of impact.
* Contre-coup: Injury occurs on the opposite side of the brain from the impact site.
citation: Page 89 (Book Page): [produces a 'contre-coup' injury opposite the site of impact... 'coup' lesion at the site of impact.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: What is 'Traumatic Delayed Apoplexy' in the context of brain injuries?
back: * Intra-cerebral hemorrhage occurring in a healthy individual after a latent interval (days to weeks) following trauma.
citation: Page 91 (Book Page): [If the interval is more, it is called delayed traumatic apoplexy... any interval longer than three weeks suggests a spontaneous hemorrhage.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: Describe the 'Black Eye' phenomenon following forehead trauma.
back: * Gravity shifting of extravasated blood from the forehead/scalp along tissue lines to the orbital region within 24 hours.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [Gravity shifting of blood of injury to forehead later causing black eye... within first 24 hours.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: List the diagnostic findings of 'Shajjah-i-Munaqqilah' and 'Shajjah-i-Ammah'.
back:
* Munaqqilah: Fracturing bone with displacement.
* Ammah: Fracturing bone with a wound touching the brain membranes (dura mater).
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): [Shajjah-i-Munaqqilah: Fracturing of bone with displacement. Shajjah-i-Ammah: Fracturing of bone and the wound touching the membranes of brain.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: Define "Hurt" according to the Qisas and Diyat Ordinance.
back: Causing pain, harm, disease, infirmity, injury or impairing, disabling, or dismembering any organ of the body or part thereof without causing death.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): Hurt is defined as and means causing of pain, harm, disease, infirmity, injury or impairing, disabling, dismembering any organ of the body or part thereof withoutt causing death.

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: Explain the pathological difference between Shajjah-i-Mudihah and Shajjah-i-Hashimah.
back:
• Shajjah-i-Mudihah: Exposing of bone without fracture.
• Shajjah-i-Hashimah: Fracturing of bone without displacement.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): Shajjah-i-Mudihah: Exposing of bone withoutt its fracture. Shajjah-i-Hashimah: Fracturing of bone withoutt displacement.

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: Contrast "Jaifah" and "Ghayr-jaifah" hurts based on anatomical extension.
back:
• Jaifah: Hurt extending into the body cavity of the trunk.
• Ghayr-jaifah: Hurt on the body (other than head/face) not extending into a body cavity.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): Jaifah: Hurt extending to the body cavity of the trunk. Ghayr-jaifah: Hurt on part of the body other than the head and face... not amounting to Jaifah.

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: A victim presents with a facial wound involving a displaced fracture. How is this classified?
back:
Shajjah-i-Munaqqilah.
• Defined as fracturing of bone with displacement.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): Shajjah-i-Munaqqilah: Fracturing of bone with displacement.

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: What is the medicolegal significance of the "Rice-Water" stools observation in suspected poisoning?
back: It is a hallmark of acute Arsenic poisoning, simulating the clinical presentation of Cholera.
citation: Page 173 (Book Page): Bulk of transudes into the lumen of small intestine... leads to characteristic rice water stools.

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: Define "Itlaf-i-Udw" in the context of regional trauma.
back: Causing dismemberment, amputation, or severment of any limb or organ of the body.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): Itlaf-i-udw: Causing of dismemberment, amputation, severement of any limb or organ of the badly [body].

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: Differentiate between Arsh and Daman as forms of legal compensation.
back:
• Arsh: Compensation specified in law for causing specific hurts.
• Daman: Compensation not specified in law, determined by the court.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): Arsh: Compensation specified in law for causing hurt... Daman: Compensation not liable to Arsh and to be determined by the court.

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: A corpse has a deep neck wound with multiple superficial "Hesitation Cuts." What is the likely manner of death?
back:
Suicide (Cut-throat).
• Hesitation cuts are typical of self-inflicted wounds, located near the initiation point.
citation: Page 80 (Book Page): Hesitation cuts: Near initiation point [Suicidal]... Usually single [Homicidal].

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: Describe the chronologic color changes in a bruise to estimate the age of an injury.
back:
• 0-2 Days: Purple/dark red.
• 4-5 Days: Greenish.
• 7-10 Days: Yellowish.
• Disappears: Within 2 weeks.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): Recent bruise appears purple... greenish in about four/five days... yellow within seven to ten days and finally disappears.

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: Which specific body regions are involved in Shajjah injuries?
back: The head and the face only.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): Shajjah: Hurt on the head or face which does not amount to itlaf-i-Udw.

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: How does the Qisas and Diyat Ordinance distinguish the terms 'wound' and 'hurt'?
back:
- Wound: Any break in body tissue (internal or external).
- Hurt: Legal term for pain, illness, or disabling an organ without causing death.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): [From medical point of view. any break in the body tissue, externally or internally is termed as wound or injury... Law has not defined word wound so far and prefers to use the term hurt for it instead... Hurt is defined as and means causing of pain, harm, disease, infirmity, injury or impairing, disabling, dismembering any organ of the body or part thereof withoutt causing death.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: Describe the mechanism of the 'blowback phenomenon' in regional firearm entry wounds.
back:
- Occurs when gas enters tissues over hard bone (scalp/face).
- Bone resists expansion, forcing gases back, causing a stellate, ragged wound with everted margins.
citation: Page 72 (Book Page): [When there is hard bone as in scalp or cheek, it resists entry of gases, which return with extreme force; blowback phenomenon causing stellate or ragged wound with everted margin.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: What is the primary diagnostic contrast between ante-mortem and post-mortem abrasions?
back:
- Ante-mortem: Exhibits 'vital reaction' including redness, swelling, or inflammation.
- Post-mortem: Lacks inflammation; turns brown and parchment-like with time after drying.
citation: Page 55 (Book Page): [Postmortem abrasion may be confused with ante-mortem abrasion especially when on Vital region like neck... Anle-moriem abrasion shows vital reaction... Post-mortem abrasion with passage of time after drying nt appearance.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: A victim presents with a 'black eye' following forehead trauma. Explain the medicolegal mechanism.
back:
- Gravity shifting: Effused blood tracks from the forehead along tissue lines of least resistance.
- Settles in the lax peri-orbital tissues within 24 hours.
citation: Page 56 (Book Page): [Gravity shifting of bruise occurs from its inig, site along tissue line of least resistance to ben region under the influence of gravity within firs, +; hours. It changes both its position and shape, noticed following 4 blow on the forehead/scalp 2,, later causing black eve.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: Which biochemical markers detect ante-mortem burns before histological changes appear?
back:
- Increased activity of specific enzymes at the burn periphery:
- Alkaline phosphatase, acid phosphatase, non-specific esterase, and Lucien amino-peptidase.
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): [Increase in enzyme reaction at the periphery of the burn, which can be detected much earlier than histological changes... Chosen study enzymes were alkaline phosphatase, acid phosphatase, Lucien amino-peptidase and non-specific esterase.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: What are the three defining macroscopic criteria of a lacerated wound?
back:
- Irregular, bruised margins.
- Bridging tissue tags (nerves/vessels) across the wound floor.
- Crushed hair bulbs or hair forced into the wound.
citation: Page 57 (Book Page): [Main characteristics of a lacerated wound are varied shapes with imegular margins, | define @ngles and walls that have bndging tissue tags and hair in bearing area may get pushed into i with tage biléserished.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: What is the conceptual significance of 'hesitation cuts' in medicolegal wounding?
back:
- Multiple, superficial, parallel incisions near a deep lethal wound.
- Diagnostic hallmark of suicidal intent and self-inflicted regional injury.
citation: Page 80 (Book Page): [Hesitation cuts are superficial cuts at Point Of initiation followed by final deep lethal wound jn suicide.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: Differentiate suicidal from homicidal cut-throat injuries regarding wound depth and tailing.
back:
- Suicidal: Maximum depth at initiation; tails off at end; hesitation cuts present.
- Homicidal: Deepest in the middle or uniformly deep; no tailing; hesitation cuts absent.
citation: Page 80 (Book Page): [Table 7.5... Suicidal... Depth of wound Maximum at the pom of initiation... Tailing Present on working hand side... Homicidal... Maximum depth im the middle... Tailing Absent.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: Describe the physiological loop leading to death in manual strangulation (throttling).
back:
- Compression of the carotid sinus stimulates the vagus nerve.
- Triggers parasympathetic over-stimulation, causing reflex bradycardia, hypotension, and sudden cardiac arrest.
citation: Page 154 (Book Page): [Increased tension precipitates strong parasympathetic stunulation and produces inhibitory circulatory effects such as slowing of pulse... and asystole... leading to circulatory failure, which proves fatal.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: Describe the anatomic location and direction of a typical hanging ligature mark.
back:
- Location: Usually high up in the neck, above the thyroid cartilage.
- Direction: Oblique, running upward toward the knot.
citation: Page 152 (Book Page): [Direction of the mark is G5: oblique going upward towards the knot. It a1 my imprint abrasion usually situated in upper part of the neck above thyroid cartilage.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: Define 'Arsh' according to the Qisas and Diyat Ordinance.
back:
- Compensation specified in law for causing hurt.
- Payable by the offender to the victim or their heirs.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): [Arsh: Compensation specified in law for causing hurt payable to the victim or his heirs by the offender.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: What is the specific medicolegal definition of 'Shajjah'?
back:
- Any hurt caused on the head or face.
- Does not amount to Itlaf-i-Udw or Itlaf-i-Salahiyyat-i-Udw.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): [Shajjah: Hurt on the head or face which does not amount to itlaf-i-Udw or itlaf-i-Salahiyyat-i-Udw.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: Distinguish between 'Jaifah' and 'Ghayr-jaifah' hurts.
back:
- Jaifah: Hurt extending into the body cavity of the trunk.
- Ghayr-jaifah: Hurt on parts other than head/face not extending into a body cavity.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): [Jaifah: Hurt extending to the body cavity of the trunk. Ghayr-jaifah: Hurt on part of the body other than the head and face bearing mark of wound which may be... Hurt not amounting to Jaifah.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: Classify a face injury that exposes the bone without causing a fracture.
back:
- Shajjah-i-Mudihah.
- Defined as exposing bone without fracture.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): [Shajjah-i-Mudihah: Exposing of bone without its fracture.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: Define 'Itlaf-i-Salahiyyat-i-Udw' in regional injury assessment.
back:
- Destroying or permanently impairing the function/capacity of an organ.
- Causing permanent disfigurement.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): [Itlaf-i-Salahiyyat-i-Udw: Destroying of permanently impairing the function or capacity of an organ of the body or causing permanent disfigurement.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: How is 'Shajjah-i-Damighah' clinically defined in medicolegal reports?
back:
- A fracture of the skull bone.
- Accompanied by the rupture of the brain membranes.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): [Shajjah-i-Damighah: Fracturing of bone with rupturing of the brain membranes.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: Distinguish 'Shajjah-i-Hashimah' from 'Shajjah-i-Munaqqilah'.
back:
- Hashimah: Fracture of bone without displacement.
- Munaqqilah: Fracture of bone with displacement.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): [Shajjah-i-Hashimah: Fracturing of bone without displacement. Shajjah-i-Munaqqilah: Fracturing of bone with displacement.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: Define 'Mutalahimah' under the Ghayr-jaifah injury category.
back:
- A hurt on a part of the body other than head/face.
- Characterized by the laceration of the flesh.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): [Mutalahimah: Lacerating of the flesh.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: What defines 'Shajjah-i-Ammah' regarding its depth?
back:
- A fracture of the skull bone.
- The wound touches the membranes of the brain (dura mater).
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): [Shajjah-i-Ammah: Fracturing of bone and the wound touching the membranes of brain.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: What is the medicolegal term for the 'rupturing of the skin with bleeding'?
back:
- Damiyah.
- It is the first subtype of Ghayr-jaifah injury.
citation: Page 27 (Book Page): [Damiyah: Rupturing of the skin with bleeding.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: Define 'Hurt' as per the Qisas and Diyat Ordinance.
back: Causing pain, harm, disease, infirmity, or injury, or impairing, disabling, or dismembering any organ or part without causing death.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): [Hurt is defined as and means causing of pain, harm, disease, infirmity, injury or impairing, disabling, dismembering any organ of the body or part thereof withoutt causing death.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: Explain the 'Contre-coup' mechanism in traumatic head injuries.
back: Injury occurring to the brain on the side opposite the site of impact. It results from the brain stretching or moving within the cranial cavity.
citation: Page 90 (Book Page): [Contre-coup mechanism... has been known to stretch the brain tissue. ... Site of coup injury is that where force has been applied.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: Contrast a Bruise with Postmortem Lividity (Hypostasis) on incision.
back:
* Bruise: Extra-vascular blood (clotted, not washable); vital reaction present.
* Hypostasis: Intra-vascular blood (washes away with water); no vital reaction.
citation: Page 60 (Book Page): [Table 6.3: Bruise (Anti-mortem) ... Blood vessels are broken and blood is present in inter-statius tissue. ... Postmortem Lividity ... Blood is within the vessels and when incised, flows out.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: A victim presents with a transverse, continuous neck groove of uniform depth. Diagnosis?
back: Ligature Strangulation. The horizontal direction and uniform depth distinguish it from the oblique, non-continuous mark of hanging.
citation: Page 83 (Book Page): [strangulation with hard material showing acute facial congestion, horizontal and continuous ligature mark of uniform depth all around neck.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: What is the medicolegal significance of 'Vagal Inhibition' in neck pressure?
back: Sudden stimulation of the carotid sinus or vagus nerve leads to immediate reflex cardiac arrest and death, often showing minimal external signs of asphyxia.
citation: Page 96 (Book Page): [Death from vagal shock occurs ... Application of stimulus to neck of the womb is like injuries to larynx or trachea. It is capable of precipitating Vagal inhibition and sudden arrest of heart.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: Define 'Arsh' as a form of legal compensation for injury.
back: The compensation specified in the law for causing specific types of hurt, payable by the offender to the victim or their heirs.
citation: Page 30 (Book Page): [Arsh: Compensation specified in law for causing hurt by the offender to the victim or his heirs.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: Distinguish 'Hesitation Cuts' in suicidal vs. homicidal injuries.
back:
* Suicidal: Multiple superficial cuts at the wound's initiation point.
* Homicidal: Usually absent; wounds are typically bold and deep from the start.
citation: Page 80 (Book Page): [Suicidal cutthroat ... Hesitation cuts at point of initiation ... Homicidal cutthroat ... Hesitation cut: Absent.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: Differentiate a 'Split Laceration' from an incised wound on the scalp.
back:
* Split Laceration: Irregular margins, bridging tissue tags, crushed hair bulbs.
* Incised Wound: Clean-cut margins, no tissue tags, hair bulbs are cleanly cut.
citation: Page 60 (Book Page): [Split, also called crush laceration ... may resemble an incision wound ... margins and bulbs of hair are crushed. ... bridging tissue tags and hair in bearing area may get pushed into i.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: What is the most common site and source of Extradural Hemorrhage (EDH)?
back:
Site: Temporal fossa.
Source: Rupture of the middle meningeal artery or vein, often secondary to a skull fracture.
citation: Page 90 (Book Page): [The most common site of extradural hemorrhage is temporal fossa due to the rupture of middle meningeal vessels.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: List the defining characteristics of a 'Greenstick Fracture'.
back:
* Incomplete fracture (one side of bone broken).
* Common in children due to high bone elasticity.
* Results from slight force exceeding partial bone strength.
citation: Page 60 (Book Page): [Long bones of children are comparatively more elastic and show less damage to only one side of bone resulting in green stick — fracture.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: Define the two mechanical types of cerebral concussion based on head movement.
back:
1. Acceleration concussion: Moving object strikes stationary head.
2. Deceleration concussion: Moving head strikes stationary object (generally severer).
citation: Page 89 (Book Page): [Concussion... is of two types: Acceleration concussion which occurs following a strike to the stationary head and Deceleration concussion which is caused by the moving head hitting a stationary object, it is severer of the two.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: Explain the 'General Deformation' mechanism of skull fracturing.
back: The skull is compressed in one plane, behaves like an elastic sphere, and bulges/fractures in the opposite plane.
citation: Page 61 (Book Page): [General deformation of whole skull occurs due to compression of the skull. When skull is compressed in one plane, it behaves as an elastic sphere and bulges out in other plane. where fracture occurs.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: Distinguish between Antegrade and Retrograde amnesia in regional head trauma.
back:
1. Antegrade: Memory loss extending forwards from the time of injury.
2. Retrograde: Memory loss extending backwards from the moment of regaining consciousness.
citation: Page 89 (Book Page): [Post-traumatic amnesia is of two types: Antrograde amnesia extending forwards from the time of injury. Retrograde amnesia extending backwards from the time of regaining consciousness.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: Case: A victim regains consciousness after head trauma but later lapses into a fatal coma. Diagnosis?
back: Extradural Hemorrhage (EDH). It is characterized by a 'lucid interval' before the onset of brain compression symptoms.
citation: Page 90 (Book Page): [Extradural hemorrhage... symptoms of compression manifest after an interval of few hours and this interval is called lucid interval.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: Describe the 'Contre-coup' mechanism of internal brain injury.
back: Brain injury occurs at a site diametrically opposite to the point of impact due to brain movement and stretching.
citation: Page 90 (Book Page): [Contre-coup... injury on the brain after a strike to the mobile head. Site of coup injury is a direct consequence of trauma... Effects on the brain are immediate because force has been applied.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: What is the most common anatomical site for an Extradural hemorrhage?
back: The temporal fossa, typically resulting from the rupture of the middle meningeal artery or vein.
citation: Page 90 (Book Page): [The most common site of extradural hemorrhage is temporal fossa due to the rupture of middle meningeal vessels.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: Contrast 'Lucid Intervals' in EDH with 'Latent Forms' in Subdural Hemorrhage (SDH).
back:
1. EDH: Lucid interval lasts hours (arterial).
2. SDH: Latent forms involve slow venous leakage, potentially remaining asymptomatic for months/years (blood cysts).
citation: Page 91 (Book Page): [Latent form of subdural hemorrhage develops due to slow leakage from a perforating vein. No symptom of this mishap appears... Subdural hematoma eventually becomes a blood cyst, which remains so for months or even years.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: Differentiate Traumatic from Spontaneous Intracerebral Hemorrhage based on location.
back:
1. Traumatic: Usually in frontal or temporal white matter.
2. Spontaneous: Usually in the basal ganglia regions (associated with hypertension/aneurysms).
citation: Page 92 (Book Page): [Location of post-traumatic hemorrhage is usually in white matter of frontal and temporal region... Spontaneous hemorrhage is usually in the ganglion regions in a patient who is overweight and has a history of high blood pressure.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: Explain the cardiovascular response to increased tension in the carotid sinus during neck compression.
back: Strong parasympathetic stimulation occurs, causing inhibitory effects: slowed pulse, depressed myocardial contractility, and generalized vasodilation.
citation: Page 154 (Book Page): [Increased tension... precipitates strong parasympathetic stimulation and produces inhibitory circulatory effects such as slowing of pulse, depression of myocardial contractility and conductivity and generalized vasodilatation.]

category: Describe medicolegal aspects of regional injuries
front: Q: Which specific laryngeal structures are most commonly fractured during manual strangulation?
back: The greater cornua of the hyoid bone and the superior horn of the thyroid cartilage (especially when calcified).
citation: Page 150 (Book Page): [Common sites of fractures are greater cornue of hyoid bone and superior horn of thyroid cartilage especially when calcified as in advanced age.]

category: Classify transport accidents
front: Q: What are the three primary modes of travel used to classify transport accidents?
back:
1. Road (most frequent)
2. Rail
3. Air
citation: Page 86 (Book Page): Traffic accidents have been investigated from point of view of mode of travels i.e. road, rail and air.

category: Classify transport accidents
front: Q: Classify road-traffic accidents based on the number of vehicles and direction.
back:
1. Number: Single or multiple vehicles.
2. Direction: Frontal, lateral, or rear impact.
citation: Page 86 (Book Page): Table 8.3: Type of road-traffic accidents: Number of vehicles involved—Single or more vehicles; Direction of the impact—Frontal, lateral and rear impact

category: Classify transport accidents
front: Q: Distinguish between 'Moderate' and 'Severe' transport injuries for medical certification.
back:
1. Moderate: Serious injuries requiring one week of hospitalization.
2. Severe: Life-endangering injuries requiring more than one week of hospitalization.
citation: Page 86 (Book Page): Moderate (injuries serious, victim hospitalized for a week); Severe (injuries endanger life, victim hospitalized for more than a week)

category: Classify transport accidents
front: Q: Classify the three phases of impact injuries sustained by a pedestrian.
back:
1. Primary: Direct vehicle contact.
2. Secondary: Vehicle rolling/throwing the victim.
3. Tertiary: Impact with road or stationary objects.
citation: Page 87 (Book Page): Injures on the body of a pedestrian... depends upon whether impact is primary, secondary or tertiary.

category: Classify transport accidents
front: Q: How are road-traffic accidents classified by motive?
back:
1. With Motive: Homicide, suicide, or masking a crime.
2. Without Motive: Accidental (often due to intoxication).
citation: Page 86 (Book Page): Motive of accident—Crash with motive (homicide, suicide or to mask accident) or without motive (due to intoxication)

category: Classify transport accidents
front: Q: Define a 'Fatal' transport accident according to the UHS curriculum.
back: Victim death occurring immediately on the spot or within 30 days of hospitalization.
citation: Page 86 (Book Page): Fatal (victim either dies on the spot or within 30 days of hospitalization)

category: Classify transport accidents
front: Q: Classify the three main causative factors in road-traffic accidents.
back:
1. Mechanical: Engine/tire failure.
2. Environmental: Visibility/weather/traffic density.
3. Personal: Driver disability, drugs, or fatigue.
citation: Page 86 (Book Page): Table 8.2: Road-traffic accident causation: Mechanical factor... Environmental factor... Personal factor (driver)

category: Classify transport accidents
front: Q: In mass disasters with no clear order, how is survivorship classified?
back:
1. Younger survives older.
2. Male survives female.
3. Healthy survives diseased.
citation: Page 93 (Book Page): presumption of law of survivorship is that: Younger in age shall survive the older; Male shall survive the female; Healthy shall survive the diseased

category: Classify transport accidents
front: Q: Where are primary impact injuries typically located on a pedestrian?
back: On the legs, thighs, or hips (corresponding to vehicle bumper height).
citation: Page 87 (Book Page): Primary impact injuries are situated on legs, thighs or hips

category: Classify transport accidents
front: Q: What defines a 'Minor' injury in transport accident classification?
back: Injuries are trivial and the victim does not require hospitalization.
citation: Page 86 (Book Page): Minor (injuries trivial, victim not hospitalized)

category: Classify transport accidents
front: Q: Classify transport accidents based on the mode of travel.
back:
1. Road accidents
2. Rail accidents
3. Air accidents
citation: Page 86 (Book Page): Traffic accidents have been investigated from point of view of mode of travels i.e. road, rail and air.

category: Classify transport accidents
front: Q: Classify road traffic accidents based on the number of vehicles involved.
back:
1. Single-vehicle accidents
2. Multiple-vehicle accidents
citation: Page 86 (Book Page): Number of vehicles involved—Single or more vehicles

category: Classify transport accidents
front: Q: How are road traffic accidents classified by direction of impact?
back:
1. Frontal impact
2. Lateral impact
3. Rear impact
citation: Page 86 (Book Page): Direction of the impact—Frontal, lateral and rear impact

category: Classify transport accidents
front: Q: Case: A driver crashes intentionally to hide a homicide. Classify by motive.
back: Crash with motive. Other motives in this category include suicide or masking an accident; intoxication is considered a crash without motive.
citation: Page 86 (Book Page): Motive of accident—Crash with motive (homicide, suicide or to mask accident) or without motive (due to intoxication)

category: Classify transport accidents
front: Q: Classify road traffic injuries based on the extent of damage to the victim.
back:
* Minor (trivial)
* Moderate (1-week hospital stay)
* Severe (over 1-week hospital stay)
* Fatal (spot death or within 30 days)
citation: Page 86 (Book Page): Extent of damage to injured—Minor (injuries trivial...); Moderate (injuries serious, victim hospitalized for a week); Severe (injuries endanger life, victim hospitalized for more than a week); Fatal (victim either dies on the spot or within 30 days)

category: Classify transport accidents
front: Q: Classify the categories of victims in road accidents.
back:
1. Pedestrians
2. Cycle riders
3. Vehicle occupants (including driver)
citation: Page 87 (Book Page): Victims of traffic accident are mostly pedestrian, cycle rider, vehicle occupants including driver

category: Classify transport accidents
front: Q: List the personal factors of a driver used to classify accident causation.
back:
* Physical/Psychological disability
* Acute illness (epilepsy, coronary episode)
* Drugs/Alcohol
* Fatigue
citation: Page 86 (Book Page): Personal factor (driver)* Physical disability... Psychological disability... Acute episode of pathological condition... Drugs... Fatigue

category: Classify transport accidents
front: Q: Differentiate the three impact categories for pedestrian injury classification.
back:
* Primary: Bumper strike
* Secondary: Impact against vehicle structures or ground
* Tertiary: Dragging or run-over
citation: Page 87 (Book Page): whether impact is primary, secondary or tertiary. Primary impact injuries are situated on legs... secondary impact sites... tertiary injuries, which are due to strike against road, dragging or run-over

category: Classify transport accidents
front: Q: Distinguish between mechanical and environmental factors in accident classification.
back:
* Mechanical: Faulty engine (CO poisoning) or part failure.
* Environmental: Visibility issues, traffic density, and audio-visual distractions.
citation: Page 86 (Book Page): Mechanical factor... Faulty engine (carbon monoxide poisoning)... Environmental factor... Poor visibility... Traffic density versus speed of vehicle

category: Classify transport accidents
front: Q: What are the criteria for classifying an accident as 'Fatal'?
back: The victim must die either immediately on the spot or within 30 days of hospitalization.
citation: Page 86 (Book Page): Fatal (victim either dies on the spot or within 30 days of hospitalization)

category: Classify transport accidents
front: Q: How are transport accidents primarily classified based on the mode of travel?
back: Road accidents, Railway accidents, Air accidents.
citation: Page 86 (Book Page): [Traffic accidents have been investigated from point of view of mode of travels i.e. road, rail and air.]

category: Classify transport accidents
front: Q: Classify the three main factors responsible for causing road traffic accidents.
back: Mechanical factors (engine/tyre failure), Environmental factors (visibility/weather), Personal factors (driver health/drugs/fatigue).
citation: Page 86 (Book Page): [Table 8.2: Road-traffic accident causation Mechanical factor... Environmental factor... Personal factor (driver)*]

category: Classify transport accidents
front: Q: How are road traffic accidents classified based on the direction of impact?
back: Frontal impact, Lateral impact, Rear impact.
citation: Page 86 (Book Page): [Table 8.3: Type of road-traffic accidents... Direction of the impact—Frontal, lateral and rear impact]

category: Classify transport accidents
front: Q: Classify road traffic injuries based on the extent of damage and duration of hospitalization.
back: Minor (trivial), Moderate (1 week hospital), Severe (endanger life, >1 week hospital), Fatal (death within 30 days).
citation: Page 86 (Book Page): [Extent of damage to injured—Minor (injuries trivial, victim not hospitalized); Moderate (injuries serious, victim hospitalized for a week); Severe (injuries endanger life, victim hospitalized for more than a week); Fatal (victim either dies on the spot or within 30 days of hospitalization)]

category: Classify transport accidents
front: Q: Distinguish between the two types of road accidents classified by motive.
back: With motive (homicide, suicide, or masking crime), Without motive (accidental, often due to intoxication).
citation: Page 86 (Book Page): [Motive of accident—Crash with motive (homicide, suicide or to mask accident) or without motive (due to intoxication)]

category: Classify transport accidents
front: Q: List the categories used to classify road traffic accident victims.
back: Pedestrians, Pedal cycle riders, Vehicle occupants (including driver and un-seated occupants).
citation: Page 87 (Book Page): [Victims of traffic accident are categorized as pedestrian, pedal cycle rider, vehicle occupants including driver and un-seated occupants.]

category: Classify transport accidents
front: Q: Name the three stages of impact used to classify injuries on a victim's body.
back: Primary impact (direct contact), Secondary impact (victim hitting vehicle), Tertiary impact (victim hitting ground).
citation: Page 87 (Book Page): [distribution of injuries depends upon whether impact is primary, secondary or tertiary]

category: Classify transport accidents
front: Q: Classify the specific types of Personal Factors (driver-related) in RTA causation.
back: Physical disability, Psychological disability, Acute pathological conditions (epilepsy/coronary), Spontaneous illness, Drugs, Fatigue.
citation: Page 86 (Book Page): [Personal factor (driver)* Physical disability (loss of vision, hearing or limbs) Psychological disability (depression, mania, schizophrenia) Acute episode of pathological condition (coronary disease, epilepsy) Spontaneous illness (renal colic) Systemic disease (hypertension, renal disease, diabetes) Drugs (alcohol, tranquilizers, amphetamines) Fatigue]

category: Classify transport accidents
front: Q: What is the classification of road traffic accidents based on the number of vehicles involved?
back: Single vehicle accidents, Multiple vehicle accidents.
citation: Page 86 (Book Page): [Table 8.3: Number of vehicles involved—Single or more vehicles]

category: Classify transport accidents
front: Q: Differentiate between impact and crash accidents based on the victims involved.
back: Impact accidents: mostly occupants. Crash accidents: both pedestrians and occupants.
citation: Page 86 (Book Page): [Victims of impact accidents are mostly occupants. Crash accidents produce damage to both pedestrians as well as occupants.]

category: Classify transport accidents
front: Q: What are the three primary classifications of transport accidents based on mode of travel?
back:
1. Road accidents (most common)
2. Rail accidents
3. Air accidents
citation: Page 86 (Book Page): Traffic accidents have been investigated from point of view of mode of travels i.e. road, rail and air.

category: Classify transport accidents
front: Q: How are road-traffic accidents classified based on the number of vehicles involved?
back:
1. Single vehicle accidents.
2. Accidents involving more than one vehicle.
citation: Page 86 (Book Page): Table 8.3: Type of road-traffic accidents: Number of vehicles involved—Single or more vehicles

category: Classify transport accidents
front: Q: Classify road-traffic accidents according to the direction of the impact.
back:
1. Frontal impact
2. Lateral impact
3. Rear impact
citation: Page 86 (Book Page): Table 8.3: Type of road-traffic accidents: Direction of the impact—Frontal, lateral and rear impact

category: Classify transport accidents
front: Q: Categorize victims of mechanized road transport accidents.
back:
1. Pedestrians
2. Cycle riders
3. Vehicle occupants (including driver and un-seated occupants)
citation: Page 87 (Book Page): Victims of traffic accident are categorized depending upon mode of transport. In case of mechanized road transport... Victims are both pedestrians, cycle rider, vehicle occupants including driver and un-seated occupants.

category: Classify transport accidents
front: Q: What are the two primary categories for the 'Motive' classification of transport accidents?
back:
1. Crash with motive (Homicide, suicide, or to mask accident).
2. Without motive (Commonly due to intoxication).
citation: Page 86 (Book Page): Table 8.3: Type of road-traffic accidents: Motive of accident—Crash with motive (homicide, suicide or to mask accident) or without motive (due to intoxication)

category: Classify transport accidents
front: Q: Define the 'Fatal' injury classification in road-traffic accidents.
back:
The victim dies either:
1. On the spot
2. Within 30 days of hospitalization
citation: Page 86 (Book Page): Table 8.3: Fatal (victim either dies on the spot or within 30 days of hospitalization)

category: Classify transport accidents
front: Q: Classify road-traffic accident causation into three broad factors.
back:
1. Mechanical factors (e.g., faulty engine, tire burst)
2. Environmental factors (e.g., poor visibility, traffic density)
3. Personal factors (Driver-related: disability, disease, drugs, fatigue)
citation: Page 86 (Book Page): Table 8.2: Road-traffic accident causation: Mechanical factor... Environmental factor... Personal factor (driver)*

category: Classify transport accidents
front: Q: Differentiate between 'Minor' and 'Moderate' classifications regarding damage to the injured.
back:
1. Minor: Trivial injuries; victim not hospitalized.
2. Moderate: Serious injuries; victim hospitalized for approximately one week.
citation: Page 86 (Book Page): Table 8.3: Minor (injuries trivial, victim not hospitalized); Moderate (injuries serious, victim hospitalized for a week)

category: Classify transport accidents
front: Q: Classify types of impact sequence observed specifically in pedestrian injuries.
back:
1. Primary impact: Initial strike by vehicle bumper.
2. Secondary impact: Further contact with vehicle (e.g., hitting bonnet).
3. Tertiary impact: Contact with ground or fixed objects.
citation: Page 87 (Book Page): Mechanism of impact injuries to pedestrians depends upon whether impact is primary, secondary or tertiary.

category: Classify transport accidents
front: Q: Classify 'Severe' injuries in road accidents based on hospitalization duration.
back:
1. Injuries that endanger life.
2. Require hospitalization for more than one week.
citation: Page 86 (Book Page): Table 8.3: Severe (injuries endanger life, victim hospitalized for more than a week)

category: Classify transport accidents
coreConcept: Classification of transport by travel mode
front: Q: How are traffic accidents classified according to the mode of travel?
back:
• Road accidents (most common)
• Rail accidents
• Air accidents
citation: Page 86 (Book Page): [Traffic accidents have been investigated from point of view of mode of travels i.e. road, rail and air.]

category: Classify transport accidents
front: Q: Describe the mechanical sequence of pedestrian injuries during a vehicular impact.
back:
• Primary impact: Hit by vehicle bumper (usually legs/hips).
• Secondary impact: Body strikes hood/windscreen.
• Tertiary impact: Body strikes ground or road surface.
citation: Page 87 (Book Page): [Impact injuries to pedestrians... depend upon whether impact is primary, secondary or tertiary. Primary impact injuries are situated on legs, thighs or hips, secondary impact on back of trunk and top and tertiary impact at head hitting the ground.]

category: Classify transport accidents
front: Q: Differentiate between Moderate and Severe traffic accident damage based on hospitalization.
back:
• Moderate: Serious injuries; victim hospitalized for one week.
• Severe: Life-endangering injuries; victim hospitalized for more than one week.
citation: Page 86 (Book Page): [Moderate (injuries serious, victim hospitalized for a week); Severe (injuries endanger life, victim hospitalized for more than a week).]

category: Classify transport accidents
front: Q: Classify an accident where a driver deliberately crashes to hide a prior homicide.
back:
• Type: Crash with motive.
• Specific Sub-type: To mask an accident/crime.
citation: Page 86 (Book Page): [Motive of accident—Crash with motive (homicide, suicide or to mask accident) or without motive (due to intoxication)]

category: Classify transport accidents
front: Q: List the specific drug classes identified as personal pharmacological factors in accident causation.
back:
• Alcohol
• Tranquilizers
• Amphetamines
citation: Page 86 (Book Page): [Drugs (alcohol, tranquilizers, amphetamines)]

category: Classify transport accidents
front: Q: How are transport accidents primarily classified based on the mode of travel?
back:
1. Road accidents (highest frequency).
2. Rail accidents.

citation: Page 86 (Book Page): [Spontaneous illness (renal colic); Systemic disease (hypertension, renal disease, diabetes)]

category: Describe different factors involved in the causation of RTA
front: Q: List three psychological disabilities that act as personal factors in RTAs.
back:
1. Depression
2. Mania
3. Schizophrenia
citation: Page 86 (Book Page): [Psychological disability (depression, mania, schizophrenia)]

category: Describe different factors involved in the causation of RTA
front: Q: Identify two common mechanical failures that cause road accidents.
back:
1. Breaking of a tie-rod
2. Bursting of a tyre
citation: Page 86 (Book Page): [Mechanical failures (breaking of tie-rod or burst of tyre)]

category: Describe different factors involved in the causation of RTA
front: List the three primary categories of factors involved in the causation of RTA.
back:
1. Mechanical factors.
2. Environmental factors.
3. Personal (driver) factors.
citation: Page 86 (Book Page): [Table 8.2: Road-traffic accident causation Mechanical factor... Environmental factor... Personal factor (driver)]

category: Describe different factors involved in the causation of RTA
front: How does driver fatigue contribute as a personal factor to road traffic accidents?
back: Fatigue causes a mental block and compromises the power of decision-making, leading to critical errors.
citation: Page 86 (Book Page): [Fatigue (precipitates mental block and power of decision)]

category: Describe different factors involved in the causation of RTA
front: Differentiate between mechanical and environmental causes of road traffic accidents.
back:
Mechanical: Internal vehicle failures (tyre burst, tie-rod breakage).
Environmental: External surroundings (poor visibility, traffic density, distractions).
citation: Page 86 (Book Page): [Mechanical factor... breaking of tie-rod or burst of tyre... Environmental factor Poor visibility Traffic density versus speed of vehicle Audio-visual distractions]

category: Describe different factors involved in the causation of RTA
front: When a single vehicle crashes without obstruction, which personal health factors must be investigated?
back: Investigate driver intoxication (alcohol/drugs) and acute medical episodes (epilepsy or coronary disease).
citation: Page 86 (Book Page): [As regards accident causation... driver’s health and intoxication are of paramount importance especially with single vehicle.]

category: Describe different factors involved in the causation of RTA
front: Which specific pharmacological agents are listed as causative drugs in personal RTA factors?
back:
1. Alcohol.
2. Tranquilizers.
3. Amphetamines.
citation: Page 86 (Book Page): [Drugs (alcohol, tranquilizers, amphetamines)]

category: Describe different factors involved in the causation of RTA
front: Name three systemic diseases in a driver that serve as personal risk factors for RTAs.
back:
1. Hypertension.
2. Diabetes.
3. Renal disease.
citation: Page 86 (Book Page): [Systemic disease (hypertension, renal disease, diabetes)]

category: Describe different factors involved in the causation of RTA
front: How can mechanical engine failure indirectly lead to driver-related RTA causation?
back: Faulty engines can leak carbon monoxide into the cabin, leading to driver poisoning and incapacitation.
citation: Page 86 (Book Page): [Faulty engine (carbon monoxide poisoning)]

category: Describe different factors involved in the causation of RTA
front: Distinguish between acute pathological episodes and systemic diseases in RTA driver causation.
back:
Acute: Sudden, unpredictable events (epilepsy fits, coronary events).
Systemic: Chronic conditions affecting overall health (hypertension, diabetes).
citation: Page 86 (Book Page): [Acute episode of pathological condition (coronary disease, epilepsy) Systemic disease (hypertension, renal disease, diabetes)]

category: Describe different factors involved in the causation of RTA
front: Explain the role of physical disability as a driver factor in causing RTAs.
back: Loss of critical sensory or motor functions, specifically vision, hearing, or limb function, impairs control.
citation: Page 86 (Book Page): [Physical disability (loss of vision, hearing or limbs)]

category: Describe different factors involved in the causation of RTA
front: List the three psychological disabilities involved in the personal causation of RTAs.
back:
1. Depression.
2. Mania.
3. Schizophrenia.
citation: Page 86 (Book Page): [Psychological disability (depression, mania, schizophrenia)]

category: Classify and describe different patterns of injuries sustained by pedestrians and occupants of the vehicles
front: Q: What are the three primary phases of injury patterns sustained by a pedestrian in a road accident?
back:
• Primary impact: Initial strike by the vehicle.
• Secondary impact: Body hitting vehicle structures (hood/windscreen).
• Tertiary impact: Body striking the ground or road surface.
citation: Page 87 (Book Page): [distribution of pedestrians and depends upon whether impact is primary, secondary or tertiary.]

category: Classify and describe different patterns of injuries sustained by pedestrians and occupants of the vehicles
front: Q: Describe the mechanism and typical anatomical location of a pedestrian's primary impact injuries.
back:
• Mechanism: Direct strike from the vehicle bumper.
• Location: Usually situated on the legs, thighs, or hips.
citation: Page 87 (Book Page): [Primary impact injuries are situated on legs, thighs or hips]

category: Classify and describe different patterns of injuries sustained by pedestrians and occupants of the vehicles
front: Q: What defines the 'Secondary impact' phase in pedestrian trauma and its common injury sites?
back:
• Occurs when the body rolls over the vehicle after the primary hit.
• Common sites: Back of trunk, head, and shoulders hitting the hood or windscreen.
citation: Page 87 (Book Page): [Secondary impact site on head hitting glass of windscreen after rolling over vehicle]

category: Classify and describe different patterns of injuries sustained by pedestrians and occupants of the vehicles
front: Q: Differentiate the cause of knee and leg injuries in pedestrians versus front-seat vehicle occupants.
back:
• Pedestrians: Hit by external bumpers.
• Occupants: Hit by internal structures like the dashboard or instrument panel.
citation: Page 87 (Book Page): [injures of front seat occupant... occur in face, chin, chest, hip, knees and legs... due to structures that are fitted inside the vehicle... dashboard]

category: Classify and describe different patterns of injuries sustained by pedestrians and occupants of the vehicles
front: Q: What are the characteristic clinical findings of seat belt injuries in vehicle occupants?
back:
• External finding: A characteristic imprint abrasion on the chest.
• Pattern: Matches the width and direction of the belt material.
citation: Page 89 (Book Page): [A characteristic chest injury is an imprint abrasion caused by seat belt.]

category: Classify and describe different patterns of injuries sustained by pedestrians and occupants of the vehicles
front: Q: List the common injury sites for a front-seat occupant hitting internal vehicle structures.
back:
• Face and chin (windscreen/steering wheel).
• Chest (steering wheel/restraints).
• Knees, hips, and legs (dashboard/instrument panel).
citation: Page 87 (Book Page): [injures of front seat occupant... occur in face, chin, chest, hip, knees and legs... steering assembly, instrument panel, dashboard]

category: Classify and describe different patterns of injuries sustained by pedestrians and occupants of the vehicles
front: Q: How does a 'fixed foot' position alter the pedestrian injury pattern during a bumper strike?
back:
• It localizes the force to the lower leg.
• Results in severe fractures at the exact level of bumper impact.
citation: Page 87 (Book Page): [Fig 8.1... at back left side of leg with foot fixed]

category: Classify and describe different patterns of injuries sustained by pedestrians and occupants of the vehicles
front: Q: Describe 'Tertiary impact' injuries in pedestrians and their typical causative factors.
back:
• Caused by the body striking the road after being thrown.
• Includes grazing, dragging, or potential run-over by the same or other vehicles.
citation: Page 89 (Book Page): [tertiary injuries, which are due to impact against road, dragging or run-over by vehicle]

category: Classify and describe different patterns of injuries sustained by pedestrians and occupants of the vehicles
front: Q: What is the forensic significance of gross crushing of the head in a vehicular accident?
back:
• Pathognomonic for 'run-over' accidents.
• Often results in instantaneous death due to massive intracranial destruction.
citation: Page 90 (Book Page): [Gross crushing of head is characteristic of run-over accidents precipitating sudden death.]

category: Classify and describe different patterns of injuries sustained by pedestrians and occupants of the vehicles
front: Q: Which specific internal organs are most vulnerable to injury from a driver striking the steering wheel?
back:
• Heart (bruising or rupture).
• Lungs (contusions).
• Abdominal viscera (liver/spleen rupture).
citation: Page 90 (Book Page): [internal injury occurs... bruising/laceration of scalp... cerebral contusion/rapture of brain matter... Page 87 (Book Page): chest... steering assembly]

category: Classify and describe different patterns of injuries sustained by pedestrians and occupants of the vehicles
front: Q: How are victims of road traffic accidents classified based on their role?
back:
1. Pedestrians.
2. Two-wheeler riders (cyclists/motorcyclists).
3. Vehicle occupants (including the driver).
citation: Page 87 (Book Page): [Victims of traffic accident are classified into three groups: pedestrian, two-wheeler rider, vehicle occupants including driver]

category: Classify and describe different patterns of injuries sustained by pedestrians and occupants of the vehicles
front: Q: Name the three distinct impact phases sustained by a pedestrian in a vehicular collision.
back:
1. Primary Impact: Direct hit by vehicle part.
2. Secondary Impact: Body strikes vehicle bonnet/windscreen.
3. Tertiary Impact: Body hits the ground or other objects.
citation: Page 87 (Book Page): [Injures on the body of a pedestrian... depends upon whether impact is primary, secondary or tertiary.]

category: Classify and describe different patterns of injuries sustained by pedestrians and occupants of the vehicles
front: Q: Where are primary impact injuries typically located on a pedestrian hit by a standard car?
back: Typically on the legs, thighs, or hips. The specific site is determined by the bumper height and victim's stature.
citation: Page 87 (Book Page): [Primary impact injuries are situated on legs, thighs or hips]

category: Classify and describe different patterns of injuries sustained by pedestrians and occupants of the vehicles
front: Q: Identify the common anatomical injury sites for a front-seat occupant in a frontal impact crash.
back:
1. Face and chin (windscreen).
2. Chest (steering wheel/dashboard).
3. Knees and legs (instrument panel).
4. Hips (seat belt/impact force).
citation: Page 87 (Book Page): [In frontal impact... injuries generally occur at face, chin, chest, hip, knees and legs.]

category: Classify and describe different patterns of injuries sustained by pedestrians and occupants of the vehicles
front: Q: What is the specific forensic indicator of 'Seat Belt Syndrome' in a vehicle occupant?
back: An imprint abrasion on the chest or abdomen corresponding to the diagonal or lap belt webbing.
citation: Page 89 (Book Page): [A characteristic chest injury is an imprint abrasion caused by seat belt]

category: Classify and describe different patterns of injuries sustained by pedestrians and occupants of the vehicles
front: Q: Define 'Whiplash' injury in the context of transportation accidents.
back: A cervical spine injury caused by sudden rear-end impact, forcing the head to snap backward then forward rapidly.
citation: Page 87 (Book Page): [Rear impact produces acceleration of vehicle... producing whiplash injury.]

category: Classify and describe different patterns of injuries sustained by pedestrians and occupants of the vehicles
front: Q: Which body regions are primarily affected during 'Secondary Impact' for a pedestrian?
back: The trunk and the top or back of the head as the victim strikes the vehicle bonnet or windscreen.
citation: Page 87 (Book Page): [secondary impact injuries are situated on trunk and top and back of the head.]

category: Classify and describe different patterns of injuries sustained by pedestrians and occupants of the vehicles
front: Q: What causes 'Tertiary Injuries' in vehicle occupants according to forensic transportation pathology?
back: Ejection from the vehicle, leading to strike against the road, dragging, or being run-over by other vehicles.
citation: Page 89 (Book Page): [tertiary injuries, which are due to strike against road, dragging or run-over by other vehicle]

category: Classify and describe different patterns of injuries sustained by pedestrians and occupants of the vehicles
front: Q: Differentiate between Coup and Contre-coup brain injuries in vehicle crashes.
back:
1. Coup: Injury at site of impact.
2. Contre-coup: Injury on the opposite side of impact due to brain movement during deceleration.
citation: Page 89 (Book Page): [contre-coup, which is caused by the moving head striking a stationary object, the resultant trauma to the head is severer]

category: Classify and describe different patterns of injuries sustained by pedestrians and occupants of the vehicles
front: Q: What is a 'Bumper Fracture' in forensic medicine?
back: Fractures of the tibia and fibula occurring in pedestrians due to direct primary impact from a vehicle bumper.
citation: Page 87 (Book Page): [Primary impact injuries are situated on legs... by bumper]

category: Classify and describe different patterns of injuries sustained by pedestrians and occupants of the vehicles
front: Q: How are road traffic accident victims classified based on their role during the event?
back:
1. Pedestrians
2. Cycle riders
3. Vehicle occupants (drivers and passengers)
citation: Page 87 (Book Page): Victims of traffic accident are categorized depending upon role... into pedestrians, cycle rider, vehicle occupants including driver and un-seated occupants of public transport.

category: Classify and describe different patterns of injuries sustained by pedestrians and occupants of the vehicles
front: Q: Describe the mechanism and common body sites involved in 'Primary Impact' pedestrian injuries.
back:
1. Result of first vehicle-to-body contact.
2. Sites: Legs, thighs, or hips (bumper height).
citation: Page 87 (Book Page): Primary impact injuries are situated on legs, thighs or hips... result of first impact of moving vehicle against the victim.

category: Classify and describe different patterns of injuries sustained by pedestrians and occupants of the vehicles
front: Q: Differentiate between Primary and Secondary Impact injury sites in pedestrians.
back:
1. Primary: Lower limbs (legs/thighs/hips).
2. Secondary: Trunk and head (after hitting the vehicle bonnet/windscreen).
citation: Page 87 (Book Page): Primary impact injuries are situated on legs, thighs or hips, secondary impact on back of trunk and top [of head] hitting bonnet and windscreen.

category: Classify and describe different patterns of injuries sustained by pedestrians and occupants of the vehicles
front: Q: Which interior vehicle structures typically cause 'Occupant Injuries' during front-seat impacts?
back:
1. Seat belts (imprint abrasions)
2. Steering assembly (driver)
3. Dashboard/Instrument panel
4. Windscreen
citation: Page 88 (Book Page): structures that are fitted inside the vehicle. These structures are seat belts, steering assembly, instrument panel, dashboard, windscreens.

category: Classify and describe different patterns of injuries sustained by pedestrians and occupants of the vehicles
front: Q: What is the mechanism of a 'whiplash injury' in vehicle occupants?
back: Sudden acceleration or deceleration causing rapid hyper-extension and hyper-flexion of the cervical spine.
citation: Page 89 (Book Page): A characteristic injury to neck... is whiplash injury... produced because of sudden acceleration or deceleration.

category: Classify and describe different patterns of injuries sustained by pedestrians and occupants of the vehicles
front: Q: Classify road traffic accidents based on the 'Extent of Damage' to the victim.
back:
1. Minor (trivial)
2. Moderate (1-week hospitalization)
3. Severe (endangers life)
4. Fatal (death within 30 days)
citation: Page 86 (Book Page): Extent of damage to injured—Minor (injuries trivial); Moderate (injuries serious, victim hospitalized for a week); Severe (injuries endanger life); Fatal (victim either dies on the spot or within 30 days).

category: Classify and describe different patterns of injuries sustained by pedestrians and occupants of the vehicles
front: Q: What defines 'Tertiary Impact' injuries in pedestrian accidents?
back: Injuries sustained when the victim strikes the ground or road after being thrown by the vehicle.
citation: Page 87 (Book Page): tertiary impact injuries occurring on the side of the body hitting ground after rolling over vehicle.

category: Classify and describe different patterns of injuries sustained by pedestrians and occupants of the vehicles
front: Q: Distinguish 'Run-over' injuries from standard impact injuries.
back:
1. Run-over: Grinding compression, skin flaying, and gross crushing (head/trunk).
2. Impact: Primary strikes and secondary contact.
citation: Page 89 (Book Page): tertiary injuries, which are due to strike against road, dragging or run-over by vehicle. Page 90 (Book Page): Gross crushing of head is characteristic of run-over accidents.

category: Classify and describe different patterns of injuries sustained by pedestrians and occupants of the vehicles
front: Q: Contrast the kinematic results of frontal vs. rear-end impact for occupants.
back:
1. Frontal: Deceleration throws occupant forward.
2. Rear-end: Acceleration of vehicle throws occupant backward (relative to seat).
citation: Page 87 (Book Page): Frontal impact results in deceleration... whereas rear impact produces acceleration of vehicle.

category: Classify and describe different patterns of injuries sustained by pedestrians and occupants of the vehicles
front: Q: What is the classic external forensic hallmark of a 'Seat Belt Injury'?
back: An imprint abrasion on the chest or abdomen following the diagonal path of the belt.
citation: Page 89 (Book Page): A characteristic chest injury... is an imprint abrasion caused by seat belt.

category: Describe different factors involved in the causation of RTA
front: Q: What are the three primary categories of road-traffic accident (RTA) causation?
back:
1. Mechanical factors (vehicle faults)
2. Environmental factors (external surroundings)
3. Personal factors (driver-related issues)
citation: Page 87 (Book Page): [Table 8.2: Road-traffic accident causation: Mechanical factor... Environmental factor... Personal factor (driver)]

category: Describe different factors involved in the causation of RTA
front: Q: How does a faulty engine specifically contribute to RTA causation via mechanical factors?
back: A faulty engine can cause carbon monoxide poisoning of the driver, impairing their physiological ability to control the vehicle.
citation: Page 87 (Book Page): [Mechanical factor: Faulty engine (carbon monoxide poisoning)]

category: Describe different factors involved in the causation of RTA
front: Q: Contrast 'crash with motive' and 'crash without motive' in RTA classification.
back:
* Crash with motive: Homicide, suicide, or attempts to mask an accident.
* Crash without motive: Accidents resulting from intoxication.
citation: Page 87 (Book Page): [Table 8.3: ...Motive of accident—Crash with motive (homicide, suicide or to mask accident) or without motive (due to intoxication)]

category: Describe different factors involved in the causation of RTA
front: Q: What acute pathological conditions in a driver can lead to sudden RTA causation?
back: Acute episodes of coronary disease or epilepsy are recognized personal factors that cause sudden loss of vehicle control.
citation: Page 87 (Book Page): [Personal factor (driver): Acute episode of pathological condition (coronary disease, epilepsy)]

category: Describe different factors involved in the causation of RTA
front: Q: Which specific drug classes are recognized as personal causative factors for RTAs?
back:
1. Alcohol
2. Tranquilizers
3. Amphetamines
citation: Page 87 (Book Page): [Personal factor (driver): Drugs (alcohol, tranquilizers, amphetamines)]

category: Describe different factors involved in the causation of RTA
front: Q: List the systemic diseases recognized as personal causative factors in RTA drivers.
back:
1. Hypertension
2. Renal disease
3. Diabetes
citation: Page 87 (Book Page): [Personal factor (driver): Systemic disease (hypertension, renal disease, diabetes)]

category: Describe different factors involved in the causation of RTA
front: Q: What are the three environmental factors cited in the causation of road traffic accidents?
back:
1. Poor visibility
2. Traffic density versus speed of vehicle
3. Audio-visual distractions
citation: Page 87 (Book Page): [Environmental factor: Poor visibility; Traffic density versus speed of vehicle; Audio-visual distractions]

category: Describe different factors involved in the causation of RTA
front: Q: Differentiate between Physical and Psychological driver disabilities in RTA causation.
back:
* Physical: Loss of vision, hearing, or limbs.
* Psychological: Depression, mania, and schizophrenia.
citation: Page 87 (Book Page): [Personal factor (driver): Physical disability (loss of vision, hearing or limbs); Psychological disability (depression, mania, schizophrenia)]

category: Describe different factors involved in the causation of RTA
front: Q: What physiological effect does driver fatigue have that precipitates an RTA?
back: Fatigue causes a mental block and severely impairs the driver's power of decision-making.
citation: Page 87 (Book Page): [Personal factor (driver): Fatigue (precipitates mental block and power of decision)]

category: Describe different factors involved in the causation of RTA
front: Q: What specific mechanical failures (excluding engine faults) are listed as RTA causes?
back:
1. Breaking of the tie-rod
2. Bursting of a tyre
citation: Page 87 (Book Page): [Mechanical factor: Mechanical failures (breaking of tie-rod or burst of tyre)]

category: Classify and describe different patterns of injuries sustained by pedestrians and occupants of the vehicles
front: Q: Classify the three sequential stages of impact injuries sustained by a pedestrian.
back:
- Primary impact (vehicle contact)
- Secondary impact (further vehicle contact)
- Tertiary impact (ground or road contact)
citation: Page 87 (Book Page): [Distribution of pedestrian injuries is divided into three groups... Primary impact, secondary impact and tertiary impact.]

category: Classify and describe different patterns of injuries sustained by pedestrians and occupants of the vehicles
front: Q: Describe the physical mechanism and site of a pedestrian's primary impact injury.
back:
- Mechanical contact by the bumper
- Located on the lower limbs (legs)
- May occur at the hips in taller vehicles
citation: Page 87 (Book Page): [Primary impact injuries are situated on legs, thighs or hips depending upon the height of vehicle and seating arrangements.]

category: Classify and describe different patterns of injuries sustained by pedestrians and occupants of the vehicles
front: Q: Differentiate the primary and secondary impact sites in an adult pedestrian hit from the front.
back:
- Primary: Lower limbs/legs (bumper contact)
- Secondary: Back of trunk or head (hitting hood or windscreen)
citation: Page 88 (Book Page): [Fig 8.2: Distribution of primary impact (darker shade) and secondary impact (lighter shade) injuries to pedestrians. A. from front]

category: Classify and describe different patterns of injuries sustained by pedestrians and occupants of the vehicles
front: Q: Which specific external injury is diagnostic of restraint use in a vehicle occupant?
back:
- An imprint abrasion on the chest wall
- Caused by the seat belt during impact
citation: Page 89 (Book Page): [A characteristic chest injury is an imprint abrasion caused by seat belt.]

category: Classify and describe different patterns of injuries sustained by pedestrians and occupants of the vehicles
front: Q: What is the physiological mechanism of injury in a rear-end vehicular impact?
back:
- Sudden acceleration of the vehicle
- Results in hyperextension of the occupant's neck
citation: Page 87 (Book Page): [Rear impact produces acceleration of vehicle while it is already running vehicle and injures generally occur in the neck due to its hyperextension.]

category: Classify and describe different patterns of injuries sustained by pedestrians and occupants of the vehicles
front: Q: What defines 'Tertiary Impact' injuries in pedestrian accidents?
back:
- Injuries from hitting the road
- Dragging by the vehicle
- Being run-over by the wheels
citation: Page 87 (Book Page): [Tertiary impact injuries occur due to contact with the ground and include run-over, rolling and dragging.]

category: Classify and describe different patterns of injuries sustained by pedestrians and occupants of the vehicles
front: Q: List five internal vehicle structures that commonly cause occupant injuries.
back:
- Steering assembly
- Instrument panel/Dashboard
- Windscreens
- Door handles
- Seat belts
citation: Page 88 (Book Page): [These structures are seat belts, steering assembly, instrument panel, dashboard, windscreens, backrest and door handles.]

category: Classify and describe different patterns of injuries sustained by pedestrians and occupants of the vehicles
front: Q: Contrast the injury mechanisms of front-seat occupants versus pedestrians during a run-over.
back:
- Occupant: Often thrown out of the vehicle
- Pedestrian: Subjected to gross crushing or grinding compression by wheels
citation: Page 89 (Book Page): [If vehicle door gets opened and occupant thrown out. He will suffer from tertiary injuries, which are due to contact against road, dragging or run-over.]

category: Classify and describe different patterns of injuries sustained by pedestrians and occupants of the vehicles
front: Q: Describe the characteristic mechanism of 'grinding compression' in vehicular wheel injuries.
back:
- Body part (limbs) passed over by automobile wheel
- Crushing and separation of skin and muscle from underlying tissue
citation: Page 58 (Book Page): [Mechanism: automobile wheel over limbs... producing grinding compression of muscles. Characteristics... skin and muscles are also separated from underlying tissue.]

category: Classify and describe different patterns of injuries sustained by pedestrians and occupants of the vehicles
front: Q: Which anatomical areas are primarily injured in front-seat occupants during a frontal crash?
back:
- Face and chin
- Chest
- Hips, knees, and legs
citation: Page 87 (Book Page): [In front seat occupant including driver get injured during frontal crash... injuries occur to face, chin, chest, hip, knees and legs.]

category: Classify and describe different patterns of injuries sustained by pedestrians and occupants of the vehicles
front: Q: Where are primary impact injuries typically located in pedestrian road accidents?
back: Located on the lower body, specifically the legs, thighs, or hips. These result from the initial strike by the vehicle bumper.
citation: Page 87 (Book Page): Primary impact injuries are situated on legs, thighs or hips

category: Classify and describe different patterns of injuries sustained by pedestrians and occupants of the vehicles
front: Q: Contrast the mechanism of secondary versus tertiary impact injuries in pedestrians.
back:
Secondary: Body strikes the vehicle (hood or windscreen) after initial strike.
Tertiary: Body strikes the ground or is run over by the vehicle.
citation: Page 87 (Book Page): secondary impact injuries are situated on back of trunk, shoulder and top and tertiary impact at head hitting ground... dragging or run-over

category: Classify and describe different patterns of injuries sustained by pedestrians and occupants of the vehicles
front: Q: Describe the characteristic injury pattern for a pedestrian struck from the side.
back: Primary impact hits the side of the leg/thigh. The body then rolls over the hood (secondary) and finally strikes the road (tertiary).
citation: Page 87 (Book Page): secondary impact site on head hitting hood after rolling over vehicle and finally hitting ground

category: Classify and describe different patterns of injuries sustained by pedestrians and occupants of the vehicles
front: Q: Which anatomical sites are most frequently injured in front-seat vehicle occupants?
back: The face, chin, chest, hips, knees, and legs. These result from contact with internal vehicle structures.
citation: Page 87 (Book Page): Front seat occupant including driver get injured at face, chin, chest, hip, knees and legs

category: Classify and describe different patterns of injuries sustained by pedestrians and occupants of the vehicles
front: Q: Differentiate the physics of frontal versus rear impacts for vehicle occupants.
back:
Frontal: Body decelerates into the vehicle interior.
Rear: The vehicle accelerates into the occupant’s relatively stationary body.
citation: Page 87 (Book Page): Frontal impact produces deceleration... Rear impact produces acceleration of vehicle against relatively [stationary] body
