category: Classify thermal injuries-flame burns and scalds
front: Q: Define the 'Pugilistic Attitude' found in burnt corpses.
back:
• A 'boxer' posture.
• Mechanism: Heat coagulation and shortening of flexor muscle proteins.
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [Dead body acquires a specific boxer attitude called pugilistic attitude due to heat coagulation and shortening of flexor muscle proteins.]

category: Classify thermal injuries-flame burns and scalds
front: Q: What defines the 'vital reaction' in a burn injury to distinguish it from post-mortem heat exposure?
back:
• Erythema (reddening) about 1/4 inch wide bordering the lesion.
• Presence of leucocyte infiltration on microscopy.
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): [Heated objects and flame produce well marked reddening, 1/4 inch in width, bordering the lesion... Burnt skin shows leucocytes infiltration.]

category: Classify thermal injuries-flame burns and scalds
front: Q: Apply the 'Rule of Nine' to calculate burn surface area for the trunk.
back:
• Front of chest and abdomen: 18% (9% each).
• Back of chest and abdomen/buttocks: 18% (9% each).
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [Table 6.7: Front of chest 9%, Back of chest 9%, Front of abdomen 9%, Back of abdomen and buttocks 9%.]

category: Classify thermal injuries-flame burns and scalds
front: Q: Differentiate an extra-dural heat hematoma from a traumatic extra-dural hemorrhage.
back:
• Heat Hematoma: Light color and characteristic 'honeycomb' appearance.
• Occurs in the vicinity of external head burns.
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [extra-dural heat hematoma... hematoma is light in color and has a honeycomb appearance.]

category: Classify thermal injuries-flame burns and scalds
front: Q: Identify the specific gastrointestinal complication of severe thermal burns.
back:
• Curling’s ulcers.
• Occur in gastric and duodenal mucosa due to stress and pain.
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [Curling ulcers develop in gastric and duodenal Mucosa, which occur due to pain and stress of the burnt.]

category: Classify thermal injuries-flame burns and scalds
front: Q: What percentage of total body surface area involvement is considered fatal in burns?
back: • Involvement of more than one-third (33%) of the total body surface.
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): [Fatal outcome from burns occurs, when involved area is more than one third of total body surface.]

category: Classify thermal injuries-flame burns and scalds
front: Q: How are thermal injuries classified based on the physical state of the heating agent?
back:
Classified into:
1. Flame burns: Caused by dry heat/flame.
2. Scalds: Caused by hot liquids or pressure steam.
3. Contact burns: Caused by heated metallic objects.
citation: Page 62 (Book Page): [Thermal burn] includes all types of thermal lesions whether produced by heated metallic object, flame, fluids at or near boiling point and pressure steam.

category: Classify thermal injuries-flame burns and scalds
front: Q: Compare the physical texture and moisture level of flame burns versus scald lesions.
back:
• Flame burns: Dry lesions that are hard to touch.
• Scalds: Moist and soft lesions resulting from liquid or steam contact.
citation: Page 62 (Book Page): Flame and heated object lesion are dry lesions, hard to touch... Liquid at high temperature and pressure steam lesion, on the other hand, show moist and soft lesions.

category: Classify thermal injuries-flame burns and scalds
front: Q: Contrast the appearance of hair and clothing in flame burns versus scald injuries.
back:
• Flame burns: Singeing of hair and burnt/charred clothing.
• Scalds: Soaked clothing without singeing of hair or burning of fabric.
citation: Page 62 (Book Page): Singeing of hair occurs; Worn clothes show burning... [Hot liquids] Both clothes and hair do not show burning or singeing. Instead, they will be found soaked.

category: Classify thermal injuries-flame burns and scalds
front: Q: A victim presents with extensive large vesications but lacks singed hair. What is the likely agent?
back: The agent is a hot liquid or steam (Scald). Large vesicles are hallmark features of scalds, whereas flame burns typically have minimal or no vesicles.
citation: Page 62 (Book Page): Vesicles in most cases do not appear in such [flame] burns and if they do appear, their size is small... [Hot liquids] show multiple and large size vesications.

category: Classify thermal injuries-flame burns and scalds
front: Q: What respiratory finding confirms flame exposure rather than a scald injury?
back: The presence of carbonaceous (sooty) material deposited in the air passages is specific to flame burns and absent in scalds.
citation: Page 62 (Book Page): There will be deposit of carbonaceous material in the air passage [in flame burns]... [Hot liquids] There will be no deposit of carbonaceous material in the air passage.

category: Classify thermal injuries-flame burns and scalds
front: Q: Define the 'pugilistic attitude' observed in victims of high-temperature flame burns.
back: A specific "boxer attitude" caused by heat coagulation and subsequent shortening of the flexor muscle proteins, occurring regardless of whether death was ante-mortem.
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): Dead body acquires a specific boxer attitude called pugilistic attitude due to heat coagulation and shortening of flexor muscle proteins.

category: Classify thermal injuries-flame burns and scalds
front: Q: Distinguish ante-mortem from post-mortem burns based on macroscopic vital reactions.
back:
Ante-mortem burns show:
1. Marginal reddening (erythema).
2. Blisters containing albuminous plasma.
3. A pink, raw dermal surface beneath removed blisters.
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): Heated objects and flame produce well marked reddening, 1/4 inch in width... Pressure steam and liquids at high temperature cause blisters having plasma exudate containing albumin.

category: Classify thermal injuries-flame burns and scalds
front: Q: How do post-mortem skin splits differ from ante-mortem lacerations in fire cases?
back: Post-mortem splits are artifacts of protein coagulation and muscle shortening; they lack the vital reactions (bruising and bleeding) found in true ante-mortem lacerations.
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): Postmortem artifact... skin splits... differentiated during autopsy from ante-mortem by muscle shorts... [ante-mortem] accompany severe hyperemia.

category: Classify thermal injuries-flame burns and scalds
front: Q: Describe the physiological consequence of 'toxemia' in the chronological complications of burns.
back: Toxemia refers to the production of toxins by burnt tissues, typically leading to death within 24–36 hours post-injury.
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): Death occurs either within 24-36 hours due to toxemia (production of toxins by burnt tissue).

category: Classify thermal injuries-flame burns and scalds
front: Q: What is the significance of 'Curling’s ulcers' in thermal injury pathology?
back: These are acute ulcers developing in the gastric and duodenal mucosa as a reaction to the pain and stress of severe burns.
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): Curling ulcers develop in gastric and duodenal mucosa, which occur due to pain and stress of the burn.

category: Classify thermal injuries-flame burns and scalds
front: Q: Define thermal burn and its primary agents.
back:
* Lesion caused by dry heat to body surfaces.
* Agents: Flame, heated metallic objects, or pressure steam.
citation: Page 62 (Book Page): [Thermal burn is caused by application of heat to external or internal body surface. It includes all types of thermal lesions whether produced by heated metallic object, flame, fluids at or near boiling point and pressure steam.]

category: Classify thermal injuries-flame burns and scalds
front: Q: Explain the mechanism behind the 'Pugilistic attitude' in a burned corpse.
back:
* Cause: Heat-induced protein coagulation and shortening of flexor muscles.
* Significance: A postmortem artifact; not a sign of life at the time of fire.
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [Dead body acquires a specific boxer attitude called pugilistic attitude due to heat coagulation and shortening of flexor muscle proteins. Finding has no significance, as even a dead body will attain it.]

category: Classify thermal injuries-flame burns and scalds
front: Q: Differentiate between flame burns and scalds regarding hair and clothing.
back:
* Flame: Singeing of hair present; clothes are burnt.
* Scalds: No singeing of hair; clothes are soaked with fluid.
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): [Table 6.5: Flame - Singeing of hair present, Clothes burnt. Hot liquids - Singeing of hair absent, Clothes soaked.]

category: Classify thermal injuries-flame burns and scalds
front: Q: A victim has burns on the entire front of the chest and the front of the right leg. Calculate the percentage area using the Rule of Nine.
back:
* Front of chest: 9%.
* Front of right leg/thigh/foot: 9%.
* Total: 18%.
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [Table 6.7: Front of chest 9%; Front of thigh, leg & foot of right side 9%.]

category: Classify thermal injuries-flame burns and scalds
front: Q: What biochemical marker in blister fluid distinguishes a scald as ante-mortem?
back:
* Presence of plasma exudate containing albumin.
* The raw skin surface beneath the blister is typically pink.
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): [Table 6.6: Pressure steam and liquids at high temperature cause blisters having plasma exudate containing albumin. Raw skin surface is pink.]

category: Classify thermal injuries-flame burns and scalds
front: Q: List the two primary naked-eye diagnostic criteria for an ante-mortem flame burn.
back:
* Reddening (Hyperemia): A zone approx. 1/4 inch wide at the lesion margin.
* Vital Reaction: Distinguishes it from postmortem charring.
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): [Naked eye: Heated objects and flame produce well marked reddening, 1/4 inch in width, bordering the lesion.]

category: Classify thermal injuries-flame burns and scalds
front: Q: How is enzyme histochemistry applied to distinguish ante-mortem from postmortem burns?
back:
* Finding: Increased enzyme reaction (e.g., alkaline phosphatase) at the burn periphery.
* Utility: Detectable earlier than histological changes and stable after death.
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): [Increase in enzyme reaction at the periphery of the burn, which can be detected much earlier than histological changes. Reactions are stable to withstand period of delay between death and postmortem examination.]

category: Classify thermal injuries-flame burns and scalds
front: Q: A charred body is found in a house fire. What internal autopsy findings prove the victim was alive during the fire?
back:
* Presence of black sooty particles in the trachea and bronchi.
* Carboxy-hemoglobin levels in blood exceeding 70%.
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): [Presence of black sooty particles in trachea, bronchi and stomach and the presence of more than 70% carbon monoxide in blood... are strong evidence of an ante-mortem catastrophe.]

category: Classify thermal injuries-flame burns and scalds
front: Q: Sequence the physiological causes of death in a burn victim from immediate to delayed.
back:
* Immediate: Primary shock (pain).
* 24-36 Hours: Secondary shock (fluid loss/hemoconcentration) or Toxemia.
* Delayed: Infection and septicemia.
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [Immediate primary shock due to pain; Secondary shock... due to loss of fluid; Death occurs either within 24-36 hours due to toxemia... or after many days, due to infection.]

category: Classify thermal injuries-flame burns and scalds
front: Q: What is the Rule of Nine percentage allocated specifically to the perineum?
back: * The perineum is allocated 1%.
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [Table 6.7: Perineum 1%]

category: Define thermal injuries
front: Q: What is the medical definition of a thermal burn?
back: * Application of heat to external or internal body surfaces. * Includes lesions from heated metallic solids, flames, boiling fluids, or pressure steam.
citation: Page 62 (Book Page): [Thermal burn is caused by application of heat to external or internal body surface. It includes all types of thermal lesions whether produced by heated metallic object, flame, fluids at or near boiling point and pressure steam.]

category: Define thermal injuries
front: Q: Explain the pathophysiological mechanism behind the 'pugilistic attitude' in fire victims.
back: * Result of heat-induced protein coagulation. * Thermal shortening of the flexor muscle proteins causes the characteristic 'boxer-like' posture.
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [Dead body acquires a specific boxer attitude called pugilistic attitude due to heat coagulation and shortening of flexor muscle proteins.]

category: Define thermal injuries
front: Q: Contrast the effects of flame burns and scalds on body hair and clothing.
back: * Flame: Singeing/shriveling of hair and burnt/charred clothing. * Scalds: Hair singeing is absent and clothing is typically soaked in liquid.
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): [Table 6.5: Flame: Singeing of hair present, clothes burnt. Hot liquids: Singeing of hair absent, clothes soaked.]

category: Define thermal injuries
front: Q: A fire victim dies 30 hours after admission; identify the most likely mechanism of death.
back: * Toxemia. * Death occurs between 24-36 hours due to the production of toxins by the burnt tissues.
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [Death occurs either within 24-36 hours due to toxemia (production of toxins by burnt tissue).]

category: Define thermal injuries
front: Q: Which specific enzymes are studied in histochemistry to confirm an ante-mortem burn?
back: * Alkaline phosphatase. * Acid phosphatase. * Lucien amino-peptidase. * Non-specific esterase.
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): [Chosen study enzymes were alkaline phosphatase, acid phosphatase, Lucien amino-peptidase and non-specific esterase. Drawn conclusions were as follows: Increase in enzyme reaction at the periphery of the burn.]

category: Define thermal injuries
front: Q: According to the 'Rule of Nine,' what is the threshold for a fatal burn outcome?
back: * Involvement of more than one-third (33%) of the total body surface area.
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): [Fatal outcome from burns occurs, when involved area is more than one third of total body surface.]

category: Define thermal injuries
front: Q: Apply the forensic depth classifications for certifying a burn that reaches underlying muscle.
back: * Classification: Deep (Full thickness). * Defined as burns involving the full thickness of the skin and deeper tissues.
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [Generally two depths are referred to in the medical certificate; superficial, which does not involve full thickness of skin and others, which involve full thickness of skin and deeper tissues.]

category: Define thermal injuries
front: Q: Differentiate a 'heat hematoma' from a 'traumatic extradural hemorrhage' during autopsy.
back: * Heat Hematoma: Light in color, honeycomb appearance, located near external burns. * Traumatic: Dark solid clot, usually associated with skull fractures.
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [extra-dural heat hematoma... hematoma is light in color and has a honeycomb appearance.]

category: Define thermal injuries
front: Q: Describe the physiological origin of 'Curling’s ulcers' following thermal injury.
back: * Acute ulcerations of the gastric and duodenal mucosa. * Result from systemic stress and intense pain following severe burns.
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [Curling ulcers develop in gastric and duodenal mucosa, which occur due to pain and stress of the burns.]

category: Define thermal injuries
front: Q: What anatomic findings in the respiratory tract confirm death occurred while the victim was alive in the fire?
back: * Presence of black sooty particles in the trachea or bronchi. * Blood carboxy-hemoglobin levels exceeding 70%.
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): [Presence of black sooty particles in trachea, bronchi and stomach and the presence of more than 70% carbon monoxide in blood... are strong evidence of an ante-mortem catastrophe.]

category: Classify thermal injuries-flame burns and scalds
coreConcept: Physical Distinction of Flame vs. Scalds
front: Q: Differentiate between flame burns and scalds based on the condition of hair and clothing.
back: Flame burns result in singed or burnt hair and charred clothing. In scalds, the hair remains unaffected and clothing is wet or soaked but not burnt.
citation: Page 62 (Book Page): [Singeing of hair occurs: Wom clothes show burnt... In case of scalds... Both clothes and hair do not show burning or singeing. Instead, they remain wet with the type of liquid]

category: Classify thermal injuries-flame burns and scalds
front: Q: Contrast the characteristic appearance of skin vesications and erythema in flame burns versus scalds.
back: Flame burns typically present as dry, hard lesions with rare or very small vesications. Scalds present as moist, erythematous surfaces with extensive, large-sized vesications (blisters).
citation: Page 62 (Book Page): [Flame and heated object lesion... Vesicles in most cases do not appear in such burns... Liquid at high temperature and pressure... show large size vesications]

category: Classify thermal injuries-flame burns and scalds
front: Q: Define a thermal burn and list the primary causative agents.
back:
A: A lesion caused by heat application to body surfaces. 
* Agents: Flame, heated metallic objects, boiling liquids, and pressure steam.
citation: Page 62 (Book Page): [Thermal burn is caused by application of heat to external or internal body surface. It includes all types of thermal lesions whether produced by heated metallic object, flame, fluids at or near boiling point and pressure steam.]

category: Classify thermal injuries-flame burns and scalds
front: Q: Explain the pathophysiological mechanism behind the 'pugilistic attitude' in burn victims.
back:
A: A specific boxer-like posture. 
* Mechanism: Heat-induced coagulation and shortening of flexor muscle proteins. 
* Significance: Occurs even in postmortem burning (artifact).
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [Dead body acquires a specific boxer attitude called pugilistic attitude due to heat coagulation and shortening of flexor muscle proteins. Finding has no significance, as even a dead body will attain it.]

category: Classify thermal injuries-flame burns and scalds
front: Q: Contrast the condition of hair and clothes in flame burns versus scalds.
back:
A: 
* Flame: Singeing/burning of hair and charred clothes. 
* Scalds (Hot liquids): Hair is intact/not singed; clothes are soaked but not burnt.
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): [Table 6.5: Flame: Singeing of hair - Present; Clothes - Burnt. Hot liquids: Singeing of hair - Absent; Clothes - Soaked.]

category: Classify thermal injuries-flame burns and scalds
front: Q: Which specific respiratory and blood findings confirm a victim inhaled fire fumes while alive?
back:
A: 
* Presence of black sooty particles in the trachea and bronchi. 
* Carbon monoxide (CO) saturation exceeding 70% in the blood.
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): [Presence of black sooty particles in trachea, bronchi and stomach and the presence of more than 70% carbon monoxide in blood and other tissue like bone-marrow are strong evidence of an ante- mortem catastrophe.]

category: Classify thermal injuries-flame burns and scalds
front: Q: How is enzyme histochemistry applied to differentiate antemortem from postmortem burns?
back:
A: Detects increased enzyme activity (alkaline/acid phosphatase) at the burn periphery. 
* Key advantage: Appears earlier than histological changes and resists decomposition.
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): [Increase in enzyme reaction at the periphery of the burn, which can be detected much earlier than histological changes... the reactions are stable to withstand period of delay betweenn death and postmortem examination.]

category: Classify thermal injuries-flame burns and scalds
front: Q: State the percentage threshold of body surface involvement generally resulting in a fatal burn.
back:
A: Death typically occurs when more than one-third (33%) of the total body surface area is involved. 
* Trunk involvement is particularly lethal.
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): [Fatal outcome from burns occurs, when involved area is more than one third of total body surface. Most serious cases are those in which the trunk is involved.]

category: Classify thermal injuries-flame burns and scalds
front: Q: According to the Rule of Nine, what percentages are assigned to the head and upper limbs?
back:
A: 
* Face, neck, and scalp: 9%. 
* Right arm, forearm, hand: 9%. 
* Left arm, forearm, hand: 9%.
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [Table 6.7: Face, neck and scalp - 9%. Arm, forearm and hand of right side - 9%. Arm, forearm and hand of left side - 9%.]

category: Classify thermal injuries-flame burns and scalds
front: Q: Differentiate the morphology of skin vesicles (blisters) in flame burns versus scalds.
back:
A: 
* Flame: Vesicles are rare, small, and minimal. 
* Scalds: Large, extensive vesication with plasma exudate containing albumin.
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): [Table 6.5: Flame: Vesication - Rare; Size of vesicle - Very small. Hot liquids: Vesication - Extensive; Size of vesicle - Large.]

category: Classify thermal injuries-flame burns and scalds
front: Q: Outline the chronological physiological loop of complications leading to death in thermal burns.
back:
A: 
1. Primary shock (immediate pain). 
2. Secondary shock (fluid loss). 
3. Toxemia (24-36 hours). 
4. Septicemia/Infection (delayed, after many days).
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [Chronological order of thermal burn complications... Immediate primary shock... Secondary shock with circulatory collapse... Death occurs either within 24-36 hours due to toxemia... or after many days, due to infection and septicemia.]

category: Classify thermal injuries-flame burns and scalds
front: Q: Describe the macroscopic features of a dry thermal lesion from a heated object.
back:
A: 
* Surface: Dry and hard. 
* Appearance: Erythema followed by white/black coagulation. 
* Pain: Very painful; typically does not bleed.
citation: Page 62 (Book Page): [Heated object lesion is dry, which does not bleed and feels hard to touch, followed by development of areas of coagulation... very painful injury.]

category: Classify thermal injuries-flame burns and scalds
front: Q: What are the primary causative agents of thermal burns compared to scalds?
back:
* Flame burns: Caused by fire, flames, or heated metallic objects.
* Scalds: Produced by fluids near boiling point or pressure steam.
citation: Page 62 (Book Page): [Thermal burn is caused by application of heat... includes all types of thermal lesions whether produced by heated metallic object, flame, fluids at or near boiling point and pressure steam.]

category: Classify thermal injuries-flame burns and scalds
front: Q: Why do vesicles differ in appearance between flame burns and scalds?
back:
* Flame burns: Vesicles are rare, small, or minimal.
* Scalds: Show extensive, large-size vesications (blisters) containing albuminous fluid.
citation: Page 62 (Book Page): [Vesicles in most cases do not appear in such burns [flame] and if they do appear, their size is small and extent minimal... Liquid at high temperature and pressure lesion [scald], on the other hand, show extensive large size vesications.]

category: Classify thermal injuries-flame burns and scalds
front: Q: Contrast the condition of hair and clothing in flame burns versus scalds.
back:
* Flame: Hair is singed; clothes are burnt or charred.
* Scalds: Hair is unaffected; clothes are soaked (e.g., in oil or milk) but unburnt.
citation: Page 62 (Book Page): [Singeing of hair occurs: Wom clothes show burning... [Scalds] Both clothes and hair do not show burning or singeing. Instead, they remain soaked with the type of liquid.]

category: Classify thermal injuries-flame burns and scalds
front: Q: Using the Rule of Nines, calculate the burn percentage for a victim with injuries to the front of both legs.
back:
* Total: 18%.
* Each front leg/thigh area (right and left) accounts for 9% of the total body surface area.
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [Front of thigh, leg & foot of right side 9%; Front of thigh, leg & foot of left side 9%.]

category: Classify thermal injuries-flame burns and scalds
front: Q: What histochemical finding distinguishes an antemortem burn from a postmortem one?
back:
* Increased enzyme reaction (alkaline/acid phosphatase) at the burn periphery.
* These changes occur earlier than standard histological inflammatory signs.
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): [Increase in enzyme reaction at the periphery of the burn, which can be detected much earlier than histological changes... Reactions are stable to withstand period of delay between death and postmortem.]

category: Classify thermal injuries-flame burns and scalds
front: Q: Define 'Pugilistic attitude' and its significance in burn victim identification.
back:
* Boxer-like posture from heat coagulation and shortening of flexor muscle proteins.
* It is a postmortem artifact and does not indicate antemortem status.
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [Dead body acquires a specific boxer attitude called pugilistic attitude due to heat coagulation and shortening of flexor muscle proteins. Finding has no significance, as even a dead body will attain it.]

category: Classify thermal injuries-flame burns and scalds
front: Q: What internal respiratory findings differentiate a fire victim from a scald victim?
back:
* Flame/Fire: Carbonaceous (sooty) material in the trachea, bronchi, and stomach.
* Scalds: Carbonaceous deposits are characteristically absent.
citation: Page 62 (Book Page): [There will be deposit of carbonaceous material in the air passage especially if victim is trapped in flame... [Scalds] deposit of carbonaceous material in the air passage is absent.]

category: Classify thermal injuries-flame burns and scalds
front: Q: Differentiate a postmortem skin-slip from an antemortem scald during autopsy.
back:
* Scalds: Show an erythematous base with a demarcating vital reaction line.
* Skin-slip: A postmortem artifact resulting from decomposition/putrefaction; lacks vital reaction.
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): [Naked eye [Antemortem]: Heated objects and flame produce well marked reddening... [Page 148 (Book Page)] Skin slip: Postmortem artifact due to decomposition, misinterpreted as scalds.]

category: Classify thermal injuries-flame burns and scalds
front: Q: Describe the physiological stages and blister contents of a thermal lesion.
back:
* Initial stage: Redness/erythema.
* Blister content: Plasma exudate rich in albumin.
* Result: Removing the blister leaves a pink, raw, oozing surface.
citation: Page 62 (Book Page): [Progressive stages of thermal lesion are redness, which appears at once, followed by blistering of skin... leaves a pink raw surface from which fluid oozes... blisters having plasma exudate containing albumin.]

category: Classify thermal injuries-flame burns and scalds
front: Q: What is the lethal threshold for total body surface area (TBSA) in burns?
back:
* Fatal outcome: Involvement of more than one-third (33%) of body surface.
* Trunk burns carry the highest mortality risk.
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): [Fatal outcome from burns occurs, when involved area is more than one third of total body surface. Most serious cases are those in which the trunk is involved.]

category: Describe degree of burns according to different classifications
front: Q: What are the two primary criteria required for the medicolegal certification of thermal burns?
back:
1. Extent of body surface area involved.
2. Depth of the burn.
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [Medico-legal certification important criteria of thermal burn are extent of body surface involved and depth of the burn.]

category: Describe degree of burns according to different classifications
front: Q: Contrast the long-term tissue outcomes of partial thickness versus full thickness burns.
back:
• Partial thickness: Results in hypertrophied scarring.
• Full thickness: Leads to permanent contracture formation.
citation: Page 62 (Book Page): [Hypertrophied scarring occurs in partial thickness burn and contracture in full thickness severe burns, which may follow months after the injury.]

category: Describe degree of burns according to different classifications
front: Q: Distinguish between 'superficial' and 'deep' burn classifications in medicolegal reporting.
back:
• Superficial: Does not involve full thickness of skin.
• Deep: Involves full thickness of skin and deeper tissues.
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [Generally two depths are referred to in the medical certificate; superficial, which does not involve full thickness of skin and others, which involve full thickness of skin and deeper tissues.]

category: Describe degree of burns according to different classifications
front: Q: A victim presents with burns covering both upper limbs. Calculate the surface area using the Rule of Nine.
back: 18% (9% for the right arm, forearm, and hand; 9% for the left arm, forearm, and hand).
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [Arm, forearm and hand of right side 9%; Arm, forearm and hand of left side 9%]

category: Describe degree of burns according to different classifications
front: Q: Which specific enzymes are detected via histo-chemistry to identify ante-mortem burns before histological changes?
back:
• Alkaline phosphatase
• Acid phosphatase
• Leucine amino-peptidase
• Non-specific esterase
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): [Chosen study enzymes were alkaline phosphatase, acid phosphatase, Leucin amino-peptidase and non-specific esterase. Drawn conclusions were as follows: Increase in enzyme reaction at the periphery of the burn, which can be detected much earlier than histological changes.]

category: Describe degree of burns according to different classifications
front: Q: What naked-eye 'vital reaction' defines a burn caused by flame or heated objects?
back: A well-marked reddening (hyperemia) measuring 1/4 inch in width bordering the lesion.
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): [Heated objects and flame produce well marked reddening, 1/4 inch in width, bordering the lesion]

category: Describe degree of burns according to different classifications
front: Q: What threshold of total body surface area involvement typically indicates a fatal outcome in burns?
back: Involvement of more than one-third (33.3%) of the total body surface area.
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): [Fatal outcome from burns occurs, when involved area is more than one third of total body surface.]

category: Describe degree of burns according to different classifications
front: Q: Differentiate flame burns from scalds (hot liquids) regarding hair and clothing appearance.
back:
• Flame: Singeing of hair and burnt/charred clothes.
• Scalds: No singeing; clothes are soaked but not burnt.
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): [Table 13.5: Flame (Singeing present; Clothes burnt); Hot liquids (Singeing absent; Clothes soaked)]

category: Describe degree of burns according to different classifications
front: Q: Sequence the chronological systemic complications leading to death in severe thermal burns.
back:
1. Immediate primary shock (pain).
2. Secondary shock (fluid loss/hemoconcentration).
3. Toxemia (24-36 hours).
4. Delayed septicemia (infection).
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [Chronological order of thermal burn complications... Immediate primary shock due to pain; Secondary shock with circulatory collapse loss of fluid; Death occurs either within 24-36 hours due to toxemia; or after many days, due to infection and septicemia]

back:

citation: Page 62 (Book Page): [Hypertrophied scarring occurs in partial thickness burn and contracture in full thickness severe burns]

front: Q: A victim presents with permanent shortening of flexor muscles months after a fire. Name this condition.

citation: Page 62 (Book Page): [contracture in full thickness severe burns, which may follow months after the injury.]

citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [Medical Examiner takes advantage of the rule of nine to calculate the extent and percentage area involved bearing burns of the body surface.]

category: Describe degree of burns according to different classifications

citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [Face, neck and scalp ... 9%]

category: Describe degree of burns according to different classifications
front: Q: Calculate the total percentage for a burn involving one entire upper limb (front and back).

citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [Arm, forearm and hand of right side ... 9%]

category: Describe degree of burns according to different classifications

back: When more than one-third (approx. 33%) of the total body surface is involved.
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): [Fatal outcome from burns occurs, when involved area is more than one third of total body surface.]

category: Describe degree of burns according to different classifications
front: Q: List the chronological sequence of systemic complications following a severe thermal burn.
back:
1. Immediate primary shock (pain)
2. Secondary shock (fluid loss)
3. Toxemia (24–36 hours)
4. Infection/Septicemia (late).
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [Immediate primary shock due to pain ... Secondary shock ... Death occurs either within 24-36 hours due to toxemia ... or after many days, due to infection and septicemia]

category: Describe degree of burns according to different classifications

citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [Perineum ... 1%]

category: Describe degree of burns according to different classifications
front: Q: Name the two primary classifications of burn depth in forensic certification.
back:
1. Superficial: Does not involve full thickness of skin.
2. Deep: Involves full thickness of skin and deeper tissues.
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [Generally two depths are referred to in the medical certificate; superficial, which does not involve full thickness of skin and others, which involve full thickness of skin and deeper tissues.]

category: Describe degree of burns according to different classifications

back:

citation: Page 62 (Book Page): [blistering of skin... leaves a pink raw surface from which fluid oozes... blisters having plasma exudate containing albumin.]

category: Describe degree of burns according to different classifications
front: Q: Contrast flame burns with hot liquid scalds regarding hair and clothing appearance.
back:
• Flame Burns: Hair is singed/burnt; clothes are burnt.
• Hot Liquid (Scalds): Hair is unaffected/absent of singeing; clothes are soaked.
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): [Table 6.5: Hair (Singeing) Present (Flame), Absent (Hot liquids). Clothes: Burnt (Flame), Soaked (Hot liquids).]

category: Describe degree of burns according to different classifications
front: Q: A victim has burns involving the entire right lower limb and the perineum. Calculate %BSA.
back:
19% Total Body Surface Area.
• Right lower limb (front and back): 18%.
• Perineum: 1%.
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [Table 6.7: Front of thigh, leg & foot of right side 9%; Back of thigh, leg & sole of foot of right side 9%; Perineum 1%.]

category: Describe degree of burns according to different classifications
front: Q: What percentage of body surface involvement generally results in a fatal outcome?
back: More than one third (33.3%+) of the total body surface area.
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): [Fatal outcome from burns occurs, when involved area is more than one third of total body surface.]

category: Describe degree of burns according to different classifications
front: Q: What causes the 'Pugilistic Attitude' in a burnt corpse?
back: Heat coagulation and shortening of the flexor muscle proteins, resulting in a specific boxer-like posture.
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [Dead body acquires a specific boxer attitude called pugilistic attitude due to heat coagulation and shortening of flexor muscle proteins.]

category: Describe degree of burns according to different classifications
front: Q: Distinguish a 'postmortem artifact' hematoma from a true antemortem extra-dural hemorrhage.
back:
• Postmortem Heat Hematoma: Light in color with a honeycomb appearance; occurs near external head burns.
• Antemortem EDH: Solid blood clot; lacks honeycomb appearance.
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [extra-dural heat hematoma... hematoma is light in color and has a honeycomb appearance.]

category: Describe degree of burns according to different classifications
front: Q: List the chronological order of death causes in thermal burn victims.
back:
1. Immediate: Primary shock (pain).
2. 24-36 Hours: Secondary shock (fluid loss) or Toxemia.
3. Delayed: Infection and Septicemia.
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [Immediate primary shock due to pain... Death occurs: either within 24-36 hours due to toxemia... or after many days, due to infection and septicemia.]

category: Describe degree of burns according to different classifications
front: Q: According to the Rule of Nines, what is the %BSA for the anterior trunk?
back: 18% (9% for the front of the chest and 9% for the front of the abdomen).
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [Table 6.7: Front of chest 9%. Front of abdomen 9%.]

category: Describe degree of burns according to different classifications
front: Q: What are the two primary depth classifications used in forensic burn certification?
back:
* Superficial: Does not involve the full thickness of the skin.
* Deep: Involves full thickness skin and underlying deeper tissues.
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [Generally two depths are referred to in the medical certificate; superficial, which does not involve full thickness of skin and others, which involve full thickness of skin and deeper tissues.]

category: Describe degree of burns according to different classifications
front: Q: Explain the physiological mechanism behind the 'Pugilistic Attitude' in burnt corpses.
back: It results from heat-induced coagulation and shortening of flexor muscle proteins, placing the limbs in a boxer-like stance.
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [Dead body acquires a specific boxer attitude called pugilistic attitude due to heat coagulation and shortening of flexor muscle proteins.]

category: Describe degree of burns according to different classifications
coreConcept: Dry vs Moist Heat Tissue Effects
front: Q: Contrast the effects of dry heat versus moist heat on a victim's hair.
back:
* Dry Heat (Flame): Causes singeing, shriveling, and clubbing of hair ends.
* Moist Heat (Scalds): Hair remains unaffected and intact.
citation: Page 62 (Book Page): [Singeing of hair occurs... Surface hair may be completely removed by burning or may be shriveled and clubbed owing to burning and melting of the free ends.] Page 63 (Book Page): [Both clothes and hair do not show burning or singeing. Instead, they will be soaked.]

category: Describe degree of burns according to different classifications
front: Q: A victim has burns on the front of the chest and both upper limbs. Calculate the surface area.
back:
27% Total Body Surface Area.
* Front of chest: 9%.
* Both arms/hands: 18% (9% each).
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [Face, neck and scalp 9%, Arm, forearm and hand of right side 9%, Arm, forearm and hand of left side 9%, Front of chest 9%.]

category: Describe degree of burns according to different classifications
front: Q: What internal gastric finding is a classic complication of severe secondary shock from burns?
back: Curling’s Ulcers: These are acute ulcers/erosions in the gastric and duodenal mucosa resulting from pain and stress.
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [Curling ulcers develop in gastric and duodenal mucosa, which occur due to pain and stress of thermal burns.]

category: Describe degree of burns according to different classifications
front: Q: What is the most definitive macroscopic respiratory indicator that a victim was alive during a fire?
back: The presence of black sooty particles/carbonaceous material within the trachea and bronchi.
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): [Presence of black sooty particles in trachea, bronchi and stomach... are strong evidence of an ante-mortem catastrophe.]

category: Describe degree of burns according to different classifications
front: Q: Differentiate ante-mortem burn blisters from post-mortem bullae based on fluid composition.
back: Ante-mortem blisters contain plasma exudate rich in albumin, whereas post-mortem bullae usually contain air or minimal non-albuminous fluid.
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): [Pressure steam and liquids at high temperature cause blisters having plasma exudate containing albumin.]

category: Describe degree of burns according to different classifications
front: Q: Describe the characteristics of heat-induced 'flaking fractures' seen in incinerated remains.
back: These are post-mortem artifacts involving the outer table of the skull or long bones due to extreme heat/carbonization.
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [Postmortem artifact which are produced by fire... are flaking bone fracture & extra-dural hematoma.]

category: Describe degree of burns according to different classifications
front: Q: State the Rule of Nines percentage for the entire right lower limb.
back:
18% total.
* Front of thigh/leg/foot: 9%.
* Back of thigh/leg/sole: 9%.
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [Front of thigh, leg & foot of right side 9%, Back of thigh, leg & sole of foot of right side 9%.]

category: Describe degree of burns according to different classifications
front: Q: What defines the 'Line of Reddening' in ante-mortem thermal lesions?
back: A well-marked red zone, approximately 1/4 inch wide, bordering the burnt area indicating a vital inflammatory response.
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): [Heated objects and flame produce well marked reddening, 1/4 inch in width, bordering the lesion.]

category: Describe degree of burns according to different classifications
front: Q: What are the two primary categories of burn depth used in forensic certification?
back:
* Superficial: Does not involve full thickness of skin. 
* Full thickness: Involves full skin thickness and deeper tissues.
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [Medico-legal certification important criteria in thermal burn are extent of body surface involved and depth of the burn. Generally two depths are referred to in the medical certificate; superficial, which does not involve full thickness of skin and others, which involve full thickness of skin and deeper tissues.]

category: Describe degree of burns according to different classifications

* Partial thickness: Leads to hypertrophied scarring.

category: Calculate percentage of burnt surface area and their effects on the body
front: Q: Differentiate between the timing and cause of immediate primary shock and toxemia in burns.
back:
* Primary shock: Immediate, caused by pain.
* Toxemia: Occurs within 24-36 hours, caused by toxins from burnt tissue.
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [Immediate primary shock due to pain... Death occurs either within 24-36 hours due to toxemia (production of toxins by burnt tissue)]

category: Calculate percentage of burnt surface area and their effects on the body

18%

category: Calculate percentage of burnt surface area and their effects on the body
front: Q: What specific gastrointestinal complication arises from the stress and pain of severe thermal burns?

category: Calculate percentage of burnt surface area and their effects on the body

front: Q: How does thermal burn lead to secondary circulatory collapse?

category: Describe management of the burnt patient clinically
front: Q: List the chronological order of clinical complications following a severe thermal burn.
back:
1. Primary shock (pain).

4. Septicemia (delayed).
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [Immediate primary shock due to pain... Secondary shock... toxemia... infection and septicemia]

category: Describe management of the burnt patient clinically
front: Q: Which clinical feature distinguishes a pressure steam burn from a flame burn?
back: Pressure steam produces large vesications (blisters) and lacks singeing of hair or carbonaceous deposits.
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): [Pressure steam and liquids at high temperature cause blisters having plasma exudate... Hot liquids: singeing absent.]

category: Describe management of the burnt patient clinically
front: Q: Describe the clinical etiology of Curling’s ulcers in severely burnt patients.
back: These ulcers develop in the gastric and duodenal mucosa due to acute pain and systemic stress.
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [Curling ulcers develop in gastric and duodenal mucosa, which occur due to pain and stress of bums.]

category: Describe management of the burnt patient clinically
front: Q: What is the Rule of Nine percentage for one entire upper limb?
back: 9% per arm (includes arm, forearm, and hand).
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [Arm, forearm and hand of right side 9%]

category: Describe management of the burnt patient clinically
front: Q: What is the Rule of Nine percentage for the Perineum in burn management?
back: The perineum accounts for 1% of the total body surface area.
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [Perineum 1%]

category: Describe management of the burnt patient clinically
front: Q: Describe the mechanism of secondary shock in burn patients.
back:
• Circulatory collapse
• Loss of fluid
• Hemo-concentration
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [Secondary shock with circulatory collapse due to loss of fluid and hemo-concenttation]

category: Describe management of the burnt patient clinically
front: Q: Differentiate scalds from flame burns based on hair and vesicles.
back:
• Scalds: Large vesicles, singeing of hair absent.
• Flame: Small/rare vesicles, singeing of hair present.
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): [Hot liquids... Vesication Large... singeing of hair Absent... Flame... singeing of hair Present... Vesicles... small]

category: Describe management of the burnt patient clinically
front: Q: At what percentage of body surface involvement do burns usually become fatal?
back: Burns involving more than one-third (33%) of the total body surface are typically fatal.
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [Fatal outcome from burns occurs, when involved area is more than one third of total body surface.]

category: Describe management of the burnt patient clinically
front: Q: Which specific enzymes are used in histochemistry to identify ante-mortem burns?
back:
• Alkaline phosphatase
• Acid phosphatase
• Leucine amino-peptidase
• Non-specific esterase
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): [Chosen study enzymes were alkaline phosphatase, acid phosphatase, Leucine amino-peptidase and non-specific esterase.]

category: Describe management of the burnt patient clinically
front: Q: What are the two primary clinical criteria for certifying burn depth?
back:
• Superficial: Does not involve full skin thickness.
• Full thickness: Involves full skin and deeper tissues.
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [superficial, which does not involve full thickness of skin and others, which involve full thickness of skin and deeper tissues.]

category: Describe management of the burnt patient clinically
front: Q: How is a post-mortem heat hematoma differentiated from a traumatic extra-dural hematoma?
back: Heat hematomas are light in color and possess a characteristic honeycomb appearance.
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [extra-dural heat hematoma... hematoma is light in color and has a honeycomb appearance.]

category: Describe management of the burnt patient clinically
front: Q: Define the clinical manifestation of 'Curling’s ulcers' in burn victims.
back: Ulcers developing in gastric or duodenal mucosa due to acute pain and physiological stress.
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [Curling ulcers develop in gastric and duodenal Mucosa, which occur due to pain and stress]

category: Describe management of the burnt patient clinically
front: Q: What is the defining feature of a vital reaction in a flame burn?
back: A well-marked reddening (erythema) roughly 1/4 inch in width bordering the lesion.
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): [Heated objects and flame produce well marked reddening, 1/4 inch in width, bordering the lesion]

category: Describe management of the burnt patient clinically
front: Q: What is the 'Pugilistic Attitude' and its underlying anatomical cause?
back: A specific boxer-like posture caused by heat-induced coagulation and shortening of flexor muscle proteins.
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [pugilistic attitude due to heat coagulation and shortening of flexor muscle proteins.]

category: Describe management of the burnt patient clinically
coreConcept: Rule of Nine for Burn Assessment
front: Q: What clinical rule is used to calculate the percentage of body surface area involved in a burn?
back:
The Rule of Nine:
- Head and Neck: 9%
- Each Upper Limb: 9%
- Each Lower Limb (Front/Back): 9% each
- Trunk (Front/Back): 4 areas of 9% each
- Perineum: 1%
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [During forensic certification, Medical Examiner takes advantage of the rule of nine to calculate the extent and percentage area involved bearing burns of the body surface. (Table 6.7)]

category: Describe management of the burnt patient clinically
front: Q: List the four chronological clinical complications of severe burns in order of occurrence.
back:
1. Immediate: Primary shock (due to pain).
2. 24–48 hours: Secondary shock (fluid loss and hemoconcentration).
3. 24–36 hours: Toxemia.
4. Late: Infection and septicemia.
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [Chronological complications upon the body as a whole are: Immediate primary shock due to pain; Secondary shock with circulatory collapse due to loss of fluid and hemo-concentration; Death occurs: either within 24-36 hours due to toxemia... or after many days, due to infection and septicemia.]

category: Describe management of the burnt patient clinically
front: Q: Which specific body attitude is acquired by a burnt corpse due to heat-induced muscle protein coagulation?
back: - Pugilistic attitude (Boxer's attitude). - It is caused by the heat coagulation and subsequent shortening of the flexor muscle proteins.
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [Dead body acquires a specific boxer attitude called pugilistic attitude due to heat coagulation and shortening of flexor muscle proteins.]

category: Describe management of the burnt patient clinically
front: Q: What is the primary pathophysiological mechanism leading to secondary shock in a clinically burnt patient?
back: - Circulatory collapse caused by massive loss of fluid. - This results in hemoconcentration and a critical reduction in blood volume within 24-36 hours.
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [Secondary shock with circulatory collapse due to loss of fluid and hemo-concentration]

category: Describe management of the burnt patient clinically
front: Q: Contrast the characteristic appearance of vesicles in thermal burns caused by flame versus hot liquids.
back: - Flame/Heated objects: Vesicles are typically rare or very small. - Hot liquids/Steam: Vesications are characteristically extensive and large in size.
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): [Table 6.5: Vesications... Flame: Rare/Very small, Hot liquids: Extensive/Large]

category: Describe management of the burnt patient clinically
front: Q: A patient with burns on the entire trunk and both upper limbs requires Rule of Nine calculation. Percentage?
back: - Entire Trunk (Chest, Back, Abdomen, Buttocks): 36%. - Both Upper Limbs (Arms, Forearms, Hands): 18%. - Total Burned Surface Area: 54%.
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [Table 6.7: Arm, forearm and hand of right side 9%... Front of chest 9%... Back of chest 9%... Front of abdomen 9%... Back of abdomen and buttocks 9%]

category: Describe management of the burnt patient clinically
front: Q: Which four specific enzymes are measured via histo-chemistry to detect vital reaction at a burn periphery?
back: - Alkaline phosphatase. - Acid phosphatase. - Leucine amino-peptidase. - Non-specific esterase. - These detect ante-mortem burns much earlier than routine histology.
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): [Chosen study enzymes were alkaline phosphatase, acid phosphatase, Lucien amino-peptidase and non-specific esterase.]

category: Describe management of the burnt patient clinically
front: Q: What are the three chronological clinical stages of fatal complications following a severe thermal burn?
back: 1. Immediate primary shock (due to pain). 2. Secondary shock and toxemia (24-36 hours). 3. Infection and septicemia (occurring after several days).
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [Immediate primary shock due to pain... Secondary shock... Death occurs either within 24-36 hours due to toxemia... or after many days, due to infection and septicemia]

category: Describe management of the burnt patient clinically
front: Q: Why is the detection of carbon monoxide in blood significant when examining a burnt corpse?
back: - Levels exceeding 10% serve as strong evidence of an ante-mortem catastrophe. - It proves the victim inhaled smoke and was alive during the fire.
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): [Presence of more than 10% carbon monoxide in blood... are strong evidence of an ante-mortem catastrophe.]

category: Describe management of the burnt patient clinically
front: Q: Differentiate ante-mortem from post-mortem burns based on naked-eye and microscopic vital reactions.
back: - Naked-eye: Ante-mortem shows a 1/4 inch reddened border (hyperemia). - Microscopic: Ante-mortem shows leucocyte infiltration (unless full thickness) and increased enzyme reactions.
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): [Table 6.6: Naked eye... Heated objects and flame produce well marked reddening... Microscopy... Burnt skin shows leucocytes infiltration]

category: Describe management of the burnt patient clinically
front: Q: Explain the metabolic/physiological loop leading to 'Curling ulcers' in severe burn patients.
back: - Acute gastric or duodenal ulcers develop. - Pathogenesis is linked to the extreme physiological stress and intense pain signals resulting from major burns.
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [Curling ulcers develop in gastric and duodenal mucosa, which occur due to pain and stress of bums.]

category: Describe management of the burnt patient clinically
front: Q: What defines the 'Hold-on effect' seen in domestic electrical burn injuries?
back: - Occurs at 220-240V. - The current causes immediate, intense muscle spasm. - This makes it impossible for the victim to release the live conductor.
citation: Page 65 (Book Page): ['Hold-on effect' at 220-240V (domestic) causes muscle spasm, responsible for non-release of live wire.]

category: Appraise causes of death due to burn
front: Q: What is the threshold of body surface area involvement for a fatal burn outcome?
back: A fatal outcome typically occurs when the involved area exceeds one-third of the total body surface.
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): [Fatal outcome from burns occurs, when involved area is more than one third of total body surface.]

category: Appraise causes of death due to burn
front: Q: What is the physiological mechanism of immediate death occurring at the scene of a burn?
back: Immediate death is caused by primary shock, which is neurogenic and precipitated by intense pain.
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [Immediate primary shock due to pain]

category: Appraise causes of death due to burn
front: Q: Contrast the cause of death occurring in the 24-36 hour window versus after several days.
back: Death at 24-36 hours is due to toxemia (tissue toxins). Death after many days results from infection and septicemia.
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [Death occurs either within 24-36 hours due to toxemia (production of toxins by burnt tissue) OR after many days, due to infection and septicemia.]

category: Appraise causes of death due to burn
front: Q: A victim dies 48 hours post-burn with evidence of massive fluid loss. Name the mechanism.
back: Secondary shock with circulatory collapse, specifically resulting from excessive loss of fluid and subsequent hemo-concentration.
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [Secondary shock with circulatory collapse loss of fluid and hemo-concentalion]

category: Appraise causes of death due to burn
front: Q: Which toxicological blood finding serves as definitive evidence of antemortem fire exposure?
back: A carbon monoxide saturation level exceeding 70% in the blood and bone marrow.
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): [presence of more than 70% carbon monoxide in blood and other tissue like bone-marrow are strong evidence of an ante- mortem catastrophe.]

category: Appraise causes of death due to burn
front: Q: Name the specific gastrointestinal complication observed internally in fatal burn victims.
back: Curling ulcers. These develop in the gastric and duodenal mucosa due to severe pain and physiological stress.
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [Curling ulcers develop in gastric and duodenal mucosa, which occur due to pain and stress]

category: Appraise causes of death due to burn
front: Q: Anatomically, burns involving which specific region carry the highest risk of mortality?
back: The trunk. Involvement of the trunk constitutes the most serious cases in terms of fatal potential.
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): [Most serious cases are those in which the trunk is involved.]

category: Appraise causes of death due to burn
front: Q: How do respiratory findings differentiate flame burns from hot liquid scalds at autopsy?
back: Flame burns show carbonaceous/sooty material in the air passages. Scalds show an absolute absence of soot in the trachea.
citation: Page 62 (Book Page): [Hot liquids... deposit of carbonaceous material in the air passage... Absent... Flame... Present.]

category: Appraise causes of death due to burn
front: Q: What causes the 'pugilistic attitude' observed in victims recovered from a fire?
back: Heat coagulation of muscle proteins causing shortening of the flexor muscles, resulting in a boxer-like posture.
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [Dead body acquires a specific boxer attitude called pugilistic attitude due to heat coagulation and shortening of flexor muscle proteins.]

category: Appraise causes of death due to burn
front: Q: Which respiratory finding identifies smoke inhalation as a contributing cause of death?
back: The presence of black sooty particles within the trachea and bronchi.
citation: Page 63 (Book Page): [Presence of black sooty particles in trachea, bronchi and stomach... strong evidence of an ante- mortem catastrophe.]

category: Appraise causes of death due to burn
coreConcept: Immediate Cause of Death in Burns
front: Q: What is the immediate cause of death occurring within minutes of a severe burn injury?
back: Primary neurogenic shock. It is precipitated by intense pain and emotional trauma immediately following the injury.
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [Immediate primary shock due to pain]

category: Appraise causes of death due to burn
front: Q: Explain the pathophysiological mechanism responsible for secondary shock in burn victims within the first few hours.
back: Secondary shock results from circulatory collapse. This is driven by massive loss of fluid and resulting haemoconcentration.
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [Secondary shock with circulatory collapse due to loss of fluid and hemo-concentration]

category: Appraise causes of death due to burn
front: Q: Distinguish between toxemia and septicemia as causes of death based on the post-burn time interval.
back: Toxemia occurs within 24-36 hours due to toxins from burnt tissue. Septicemia is a delayed cause occurring after many days.
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [Death occurs either within 24-36 hours due to toxemia (production of toxins by burnt tissue) or after many days, due to infection and septicemia]

category: Appraise causes of death due to burn
front: Q: A victim presents with burns covering the entire trunk. Appraise the likelihood of a fatal outcome.
back: Highly fatal. Burns involving more than one-third of the total body surface, especially the trunk, carry the highest mortality risk.
citation: Page 63 (Book Page)-64: [Fatal outcome from burns occurs, when involved area is more than one third of total body surface. Most serious cases are those in which the trunk is involved.]

category: Appraise causes of death due to burn
front: Q: What specific pathological gastrointestinal lesion develops as a delayed consequence of pain and stress in burns?

category: Appraise causes of death due to burn

category: Appraise causes of death due to burn
front: Q: How is the inhalation of carbon monoxide appraised to confirm death was ante-mortem in fire victims?
back: Blood saturation levels exceeding 70% carbon monoxide indicate the victim was alive and breathing during the fire.
citation: Page 66 (Book Page): [presence of more than 70% carbon monoxide in blood and other tissue like bone-marrow are strong evidence of an ante-mortem catastrophe.]

category: Appraise causes of death due to burn

back: Flame burns show black sooty carbonaceous particles in the trachea; scalds lack these deposits.

category: Appraise causes of death due to burn
front: Q: Describe the metabolic loop leading to death from toxemia in the 24-36 hour post-burn period.
back: Tissue necrosis releases toxins into the circulation, leading to systemic toxemia and subsequent organ failure.
citation: Page 64 (Book Page): [Death occurs either within 24-36 hours due to toxemia (production of toxins by burnt tissue)]

category: Appraise causes of death due to burn
front: Q: List the two hallmark internal organ findings observed during the autopsy of an acute burn fatality.

1. Marked pallor of the liver and kidneys.

category: Describe management of the burnt patient clinically

1. Superficial: Does not involve the full thickness of the skin.

category: Describe management of the burnt patient clinically
